subtopic: FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION OF CIVIL SERVICE ACT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. J. L. BOWMAN (Dauphin) presented the fourth report of the select special committee on the Civil Service Act, as follows:
House of Commons,
Monday, June 25, 1934.
Fourth Report:
The select special committee appointed to inquire into and report upon the administration and operation of the Civil Service Act as amended, with instructions to inquire into
and report concerning the repeal or amendment of any of the provisions of the said act or the substitution therefor or addition thereto of other provisions as the committee may deem advisable, begs leave to present the following as its fourth report:
(1)	Representations have been made to your committee urging that certain temporary employees who have for long periods been occupying positions of a permanent nature should now be accorded permanent status.
Your committee find that by orders in council, P.C. 2958, dated the 16th day of December, 1920, and P.C. 3895, dated October 22, 1921, passed pursuant to the Civil Service Amendment Act, October, 1919, 4060 temporary employees who had been continuously employed in positions of a permanent character since November 10, 1919 (the date on which the Civil Service Act became law) were, during the period 1920-27, given permanent status. In 1927, however, the enabling orders in council were rescinded. The representations which have been made to your committee urge that any other temporary employees (approximately 300 in number) who were eligible to benefit under this section of the act and the said orders in council but whose permanency was not at the time effected should now be granted permanent status, in order that they may enjoy the benefits attached thereto. These benefits include the right to contribute to the Civil Service Superannuation Act, the right to receive statutory increases when these are again allowed, the right to compete for promotions when promotions are again authorized, and the right to receive retiring leave on separation from the service. A large number of the employees in question have already been permitted to contribute to the Civil Service Superannuation Act, so that the additional burden on that fund will be small, and as all statutory increases and the great majority of promotions are at present prohibited, there will be little, if any, additional^ cost in this connection nor in connection with the question of compensation, as employees will continue to receive the salaries which they are now paid.
Your committee believes that there is justification for the granting of permanent status to the employees in question, and recommends that the civil service commission be instructed to prepare the necessary regulations for submission to the governor in council to give effect thereto.
(2)	Representations have also been made to your committee that permanent status should be conferred upon the staff of the soldier settlement board, which has since 1918 been operating almost entirely on a temporary basis.
It is represented that as a result 01 reorganization the staff has now reached a permanent basis, having been reduced from a peak figure of 1,595 to a present figure of 343. The great majority of the members of the staff are returned soldiers and have been employed continuously for long periods of service-in many cases up to fifteen years. Your committee finds that in 1928 action in this respect was taken in connection with the staff of the Department of Soldiers Civil Reestablishment.	#
Your committee is of opinion that the action requested is in the public interest, and recommends that the Soldier Settlement Act be amended to provide that:

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Civil Service Committee Report
"Such members of the staff of the soldier settlement board as may be designated by the governor in council shall, notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act, be regarded as permanent employees, provided that their positions are certified' by the civil service commission, upon the recommendation of the minister based upon the report, in writing of the deputy minister, to be of indeterminate duration, and shall thereafter become subject in all respects to the Civil Service Act."
(3)	Representations have been made to your committee on behalf of employees receiving prevailing rates of pay, urging that they be allowed' to contribute to the civil service superannuation fund.
Section 2 of The Civil Service Superannuation Act limits the benefits of that act to permanent full time employees "who are in receipt of a stated annual salary of at least $600." The employees on whose behalf representations have been made could accordingly secure the benefits of the superannuation act only by having their salary r ate changed from a prevailing rate basis to a state annual salary, or by amending the provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act in this regard.
With respect to this and other matters relative to the application of the superannuation act the factors involved are of so complicated a nature that your committee was unable to obtain sufficiently definite or comprehensive information to warrant a recommendation.	Moreover the committee is of
opinion that the question is one that does not properly come _ within its terms of reference. In any case it is understood that these matters are under consideration by the advisory committee on the superannuation act to which body your committee suggests the representations above specified be referred.
(4) Your committee has been pleased to note that since the reorganization of the civil service commission substantial progress has been made in carrying out the recommendations of the special committee of 1932, and that action is being taken in connection with overlapping^and the reorganization of certain services. Your committee particularly urges that the progress which has already been made in absorbing surplus personnel and thus obviating the necessity of filling vacancies with new personnel, be extended to the greatest degree possible.
(5)	Attention has been drawn to recommendation No. 21 contained in the report of the civil service committee of 1932, recommending the setting up of a board to adjudicate upon complaints of civil servants.
It has been alleged that this board has not functioned due to the fact that no person has been designated to convere the board.
Your committee finds that the civil service commission has been dealing with complaints of civil servants by means of conferences with representatives of civil servant organizations and with representatives of the departments concerned.
Your committee recommends that the civil servant organization, of which the complainant is a member, should notify the civil service commission of its desire to have a complaint considered and that the commission then take the necessary steps to have such board convened.

(6)	hour committee has had placed before it numerous other representations containing much useful information regarding conditions in the public service in connection with all of which careful consideration has been given. It has not, however, been practicable to deal definitely with all the matters submitted and it is accordingly recommended that such matters appearing on the record not dealt with specifically by this report be investigated by the civil service commission so that where possible the necessary action may be taken, [DOT]"-hd rur^ermore that the commission submit a full report upon the matters involved to such select committee on civil service matters as may be set up at a subsequent session.
(7)	Your committee finds itself in sympathy with the representations made to it that the full restoration of promotions and increases and compensations in the service would be in the public interest and recommends that such steps be taken as soon as financial conditions warrant.
(8)	Your committee has been greatly
assisted by the evidence and information placed before it by the several civil servants' associations, and has been impressed *with the high efficiency and morale of the public service as indicated thereby.
A copy of the printed proceedings and evidence is submitted herewith.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
J. L. Bowman,
Acting Chairman.

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime
Minister) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. IS, to amend the Bank Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill extending the charters of the banks has been considered by the Senate and returned to this house with certain amendments. I propose to indicate very briefly what the suggested amendments are before making any motion with respect to them. The first section is 53, in which subsection (10) was stricken out. That subsection dealt with matters that were to be covered by the return made by the banks to -the minister, and it was requested by the Commons that the return should provide for a statement being made as to the managers and assistant managers and other employees of the banks, with a statement of the salaries which they were receiving. The Senate took the view that this w-as not a proposal cognate to the other matters dealt with by the return and that, as such information was available through the statistical branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce, it was not really a necessary part of any such return. The government is of the opinion that the view of the Senate in that regard is well taken, especially that part of their contention in which they suggest that if this were to apply to the banks it should apply equally to all other corporations created by this parliament and should be general in its character rather than special. In the committee the matter was moved by the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Morand).
The next section dealt with was section 75, which deals with the business and powers of the bank. It will be within the memory of the house that when the bill was before the committee, as well as when it was before the﻿JUNE 25, 1934
Bank Act-Mr. Bennett
committee of the whole house, a discussion took place as to the limitations upon loans made to directors and the special provision that they should not be present or vote at any meeting of the board when loans or advances were made to a director or any firm or company in which he was interested. After the bill left the committee the banks pointed out that several of the Canadian institutions have branches abroad, in France particularly, for which they have separate acts of incorporation. These are known as the Bank of Montreal (France), the Banque Camadienne Nationale (France), the Royal Bank of Canada (France), and so on, and that as the directors have to deal with the position of these branches with respect to the bank as a whole it would be very improvident, to say the least, to prevent them from being able to vote when loans or advances were being made to these branches. It is proposed to amend the section by adding these words:
but this subsection shall not apply to the consideration of loans or advances to corporations controlled by the hank, the shares of which, except for qualifying shares, are owned by the bank.

Would
that not apply to other corporations owned by any chartered bank within the Dominion of Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The bank is prohibited
from carrying on any business except the banking business.

But the
trust companies with which they are associated?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The banks do not own trust companies; there is no case in which a bank owns a trust company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That makes it unanimous The next section dealt with was section 160. It will be recalled, perhaps, that this section deals with the question of returns and matters of that kind, but no penalty was prescribed for failure to make such returns. It is therefore proposed to add the following subsection:
"(4) Every bank which neglects to transmit or deliver to the minister within the time prescribed by the treasury board a certified return showing, as to deposits by the public in Canada payable on demand and also deposits payable after notice, the number and aggregate amount of such deposits in each of the classifications by this act required, at a date to be specified by the treasury board, shall incur a penalty of fifty dollars for each and every day during which such neglect continues."
In other words, while we made a new provision for returns of this character being made no provision was made for the penalty which would follow from noncompliance with the affirmative provision of the section. The next change is to subsection 3 of the same section, where they have added the words "to the minister" after the word "deliver" in line twenty-one. That is, there was no indication, by oversight I take it, as to whom the return should be delivered. The amendment provides that it shall be transmitted or delivered to the minister, and the added words are " to the minister".
The next matter, however, may call for some extended explanation. It has to do with schedule A to the bill. Schedule A names the banks to which the act applies, namely the Bank of Montreal, the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Bank of Toronto, La Banque Provinciale du Canada, the Canadian Bank
^	COMMONS
Bank Act-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)
of Commerce, The Royal Bank of Canada, The Dominion Bank. Banque Canadienne National. Imperial Bank of Canada and Barclays Bank (Canada). Now, under the provisions of the law as applied the banks which I have just named carrying om business in Quebec may utilize the equivalent of the English name for the purpose of maintaining actions, or for placing upon their cheques or otherwise. La Banque Provinciale du Canada has the power, by its charter, to use the words "Provincial Bank of Canada". When the Banque Canadienne Nationale was incorporated by this parliament there was great difficulty in securing the name. It was felt by many at that time that the effect would be to leave the impression that that was the central bank of Canada, and that therefore probably great difficulty would be experienced, or that there would be confusion in the future if a central bank were created. The matter has stood in that way since that time, but it is quite clear from reading Hansard of that day that the charter was granted and the favourable report of the committee secured on the basis of the name being what I have indicated, namely that of La Banque Canadienne Nationale. But in view of the fact that a central bank is now being established, and that all the other chartered banks are not averse to this change being made, because they are really all directly concerned-for it might be .that a wrong impression would prevail in the minds of depositors who might select such a bank as being a national bank- it is felt that there might be added to the schedule these words:
La Banque Provinciale du Canada and Banque Canadienne Nationale hereinbefore named may respectively carry on business pursuant to the provisions of this act, under the respective names "The Provincial Bank of Canada" and "National Canadian Bank."
It would not be "Canadian National Bank" but "National Canadian Bank". That constitutes the only other amendment which has been suggested.
The history of the Provincial Bank is well known, probably because it was incorporated more recently than the old Banque Canadienne Nationale. The Banque Canadienne Nationale came into existence before confederation; in fact, it came into existence in 1859. It was first called the Bank of Hoche-laga and in 1924 obtained from this parliament the right to the name Banque Canadienne Nationale. It was made clear at that time, for the reasons which I have indicated, that it should use that name and none other. But I think the changed conditions, namely the creation of the central bank, and the removal of any objections on the part of
[Mr. Bennett. 1
the other chartered banks to the same privileges accorded to the Banque Canadienne Nationale as is accorded to them in the province of Quebec, meets . the situation. Subject to the attitude of this house, the government sees no reason why the amendment should not be adopted.

Mr. Speaker, I still think that the
amendment moved by the other house to section 75 of the bill is dangerously vague. Subsection 3 in the bill reads as follows:
In no case shall a director of the bank be present or vote at a meeting of the board during the time when loans or advances to himself or any firm, company or corporation of which he is a partner or director are under consideration.
The proposed amendment is to add the following:
But this subsection shall not apply to the consideration of loans or advances to corporations controlled by the bank, the shares of which, except for qualifying shares, are owned by the bank.
I appreciate the situation the Prime Minister outlined which this amendment is intended to meet, but I still submit the amendment is not in accordance with the sentiment expressed before the banking and commerce committee.
The other reservation I wish to make is in regard to the last words of the Prime Minister. I submit that we should not have in the Dominion of Canada to-day any bank with the appellation "National Canadian Bank" when we are just now setting up another financial institution to be known as the Bank of Canada. I believe these two names are bound to lead to a very extensive degree of confusion in future operation. I appreciate what the Prime Minister has said, that possibly as a matter of right these organizations should be entitled to use the English equivalents of their French names, but I still say that so far as observers are concerned, when they see the title: "National Canadian Bank" they will be confused, and they will not be in a position to distinguish this bank from the Bank of Canada we are now setting up. So far as I am concerned, and speaking only for myself, I wish to make these two reservations to the amendments submitted by the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I concur in the amendments to the bill. I can see no objection to the Banque Canadienne Nationale being called, as indicated by the Senate, the National Canadian Bank. As a matter of fact, there are several

Bank Act-Mr. Dupre
[DOT]translations of the names of Canadian banks. We have, for instance, La Banque Royale du Canada, which is the French translation of The Royal Bank of Canada. I do not see why we should refuse a similar translation, such as suggested by the Senate, to the name of La Banque Canadienne Nationale, so that it may be known as the National Canadian Bank. Then, there is the further suggestion that La Banque Provinciale du Canada be known as the Provincial Bank of Canada. That is a correct translation of the name, and one could not translate the name of that bank into English by using any other words. Those words, in English, indicate the title of the bank as it was incorporated by an act of parliament. Then, La Banque Nationale of Quebec and the Bank of Hochelaga were merged under the name La Banque Canadienne Nationale. That name does not indicate that La Banque Canadienne Nationale is the bank of the Canadian National Railways, and it does not mean that it is the Bank of Canada. The words "National Canadian Bank" are simply a translation of the words "Banque Canadienne Nationale." It certainly does not mean that this is a state bank. We are now considering a bill to create a state bank, to be known as the Bank of Canada, and which will operate as a central bank. I can see no reason why the name "National Canadian Bank" should not be granted, because it is a correct translation. I humbly suggest that the amendment by the Senate to Bill IS does not lead to confusion with the name of some other bank. I do not believe that when people deal with La Banque Canadienne Nationale or the National Canadian Bank they will think they are doing business with the Bank of Canada; absolutely not.
I humbly pray that the amendment be accepted, and I shall so vote.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I add a few words, in passing, in connection with the amendments made by the Senate? I quite agree with the hon. member for St. Henri (Mr. Mercier) who has just spoken. May I point out that for a long time before we had La Banque Canadienne Nationale this same bank before its amalgamation was called La Banque Nationale, which may be translated into the words "The National Bank." In my estimation that was almost as comprehensive a name as is the term Bank of Canada. For instance, at the present time we have the ringing name of the Royal Bank of Canada, and in my opinion the name of that bank is just as big and just as ringing as the name Bank of Canada. Since all the other banks, such as the 74726-269
Bank of Montreal, have translated their names -in this instance it is La Banque de Montreal -and other banks have the same right, I do not see why La Banque Canadienne N ationale should be denied that right.
This controversy is by no means new. In 1924 or 1925-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: -when the old' Banque Nationale was amalgamated with the Banque d'Hochelaga, the bill permitting this amalgamation came before this house and was referred to the committee on banking and commerce. In that committee, after considerable discussion, a vote was taken and I have a very clear recollection that those who opposed granting to the new bank permission to translate the name-I think it was to be called the Canadian, National Bank; the petition was to the effect that it should be called in English the Canadian National Bank-carried the day by one vote. The chairman of the committee on banking and commerce afterwards brought the matter to the attention of the house, and I am under the impression that a vote was taken in this chamber and that once more permission was refused the bank to call itself the Canadian National Bank. At that time I opposed the request of the bank and I see no reason why I should change my attitude to-day. There is no doubt whatever in my mind that confusion may arise and that people outside Canada may come to the conclusion that this bank is in some respects a national bank and has the backing of the government of Canada. It is I think within the memory of hon. gentlemen in this house that only two or three years ago in the United states there was a bank called either the Bank of the United States or the United States Bank, which failed with rather disastrous results; and at that time it was I think conclusively shown that a large number of people, foreigners and others who were not aware of the true significance of the name of the bank, had invested moneys in it or had made deposits in the belief that the bank was in some way connected with the American government. We have in our statutes a prohibition against the use of the word "royal," and I think at one time, many years ago, the late Sir Rodolphe Forget wished to incorporate a bank called La Banque du Canada, or La Banque Nationale-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
quite right. He did propose to call it the Bank of Canada, and that was refused.

Bank Act-Mr. Power

He did propose to call it
the Bank of Canada or La Banque du Canada, and that permission was refused by the House of Commons. Afterwards I believe he was permitted to use the name La Banque Nationale du Canada or something of that sort. I believe that the same reasons still exist against permitting any private bank to use a name which might in any way confuse depositors or investors and lead them to believe that the people of Canada or the government of Canada are in some way supporting any such institution.

With respect to the amendment made by the other house in connection with subsection 3 of section 75 I submit that this is a very proper amendment to make and one which was not visualized by the banking and commerce committee. Had our attention been directed to the necessity for such an amendment I have no doubt the amendment would have been freely granted by the committee. I see no objection whatever to the amendment and I am prepared to support it. With respect to the amendment to schedule A at page 87, granting the Banque. Canadienne Nationale, the English equivalent, I recall very well the incident brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). There was a good deal of difference of opinion in the banking committee and also in the House of Commons at that time in 1924. I do not recall how I voted on that occasion, but I do believe now that a very distinct mistake was made at that time. Just how you are going to remedy it at this stage I do not know, and I do not think it carries the mistake further by giving the bank the English equivalent. But that is the only justification there can be for giving the bank at the present time the English equivalent. They have the French nomenclature now and perhaps they are entitled to retain it. I doubt very much however whether this house ought ever to have given the bank the name which it then sought and obtained.
The question of the advisability of having given that name to this particular bank does not present itself to-day, I submit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.
It is too late.
La Banque Nationale was incorporated many years ago.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Before confederation.

Yes. When there was a fusion of La Banque Nationale and the Hochelaga bank the name was changed into La Banque Canadienne Nationale, which was no worse, if there is anything wrong about the appellation, than the first one. Now it is decided to give also the English name. Well, what is the difference? If the French name is legal, why not the English name as well? I am one of those who are not afraid of having both languages on anything in this country.

I remember quite well the discussion to which the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) has referred. I sponsored the bill in question. As regards the contention that a mistake was made in giving the bank the name which it then received, inasmuch as there is to be a central bank now I see no objection.

I certainly think this house should not agree to the Senate amendment which provides that one bank may use the name National Canadian Bank, because I am sure that name is very misleading to the general public. The name national attached to a bank conveys a wrong impression so far as our chartered banks are concerned. It is not national in any sense. I cannot see anything analogous between the use of the word royal and the use of the word national. The word national conveys in a very distinct way the idea that this is a national institution, that the nation has some financial responsibility; and in connection with a bank I think it is very improper for the House of Commons to allow this name to be used by the Banque Canadienne Nationale. I do not remember in detail the discussions that took place on this matter ten years ago, but I do remember distinctly that a majority of the House of Commons were absolutely opposed to granting to the bank the use of this term National Canadian Bank. It was pointed out that Canada would probably at some future time wish to establish a bank which would be truly national in the real sense of the word. The Bank of Canada in a sense is to be a national bank and I think the House of Commons would be ill advised to allow this change to be made.

I am glad the Senate has seen fit to amend this bill so that loans can be given to farmers to purchase fertilizer the same as they have been given heretofore to purchase seed grain and binder twine. The difficulty has been that a farmer in the maritimes who wanted to get

Bank Act-Mr. Bennett
a loan from an organization with which to buy fertilizer was compelled to mortgage his product to that organization. He was not free to sell to any one else. That may not have been a great disadvantage to him but I think the present arrangement will be better. If he can borrow from a bank he will be free to sell his product on the market and he will not be tied up to any organization and compelled to sell to them. I am glad the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has indicated that the government is ready and willing to accept this amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In moving that these amendments be now read a second time and concurred in I desire to make only one observation which I trust will not be misunderstood. If the government thought that there was the slightest likelihood of there being any confusion in the minds of either depositors or investors in connection with this bank and the Bank of Canada, it would take appropriate steps to provide against such confusion. I have been reminded by the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) of something which I saw myself- only a few years ago in the city of Dublin. There are two banks carrying on business in that city. One bank is a joint stock company and its name is the National Bank of Ireland. The other bank is the Bank of Ireland. The one institution which has been in existence for a long time is the central bank of the Free State and has fulfilled those functions as far as united Ireland is concerned the same as the Bank of England fulfilled its functions in connection with the United Kingdom before the recent treaty. This change is being made at the end of schedule A and if it is found that difficulties or confusion arises, parliament will always be in a position to deal with them. I am sure that those who are responsible for the bank will be quite reasonable in the position which they take in the matter. It must be realized that there was a Banque Nationale in this country prior to 1924. This bank and the Bank of Hochelaga united and desired to call themselves the National Bank. That was changed and the name as it now stands is Banque Canadienne Nationale, the Canadian National Bank.
Canadian national would be a poor translation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That name was thought to be undesirable as it might be thought to be a branch of the railways or the steamships. What convinced me more than anything else that there would be no difficulty about this matter was the fact that those banks which had been antagonistic to the 74726-2691
proposal in 1924 because they felt that there might be misunderstanding with respect to deposits are not antagonistic at the present time. The secretary of the association communicated that fact to me when I asked him definitely about the matter.

Because
the new bank is known as the Bank of Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Because they felt that there would be no confusion in connection with the Bank of Canada. Had there been no Bank of Canada they would not have withdrawn from their position. That is what I have been advised, and it looks quite reasonable. The question at issue now is not that of the name given to the bank in 1924. That was limited to the name in French but in view of what has transpired by the creation of the other bank, it seems to me to be unfair to say that while all other banks can use the French equivalent of their names, this bank cannot use the English equivalent of its name. The government accepts these amendments and I now move that they be read a second time and concurred in.

There is another bank called the Provincial Bank of Canada. I take it that the Bank of Canada will have branches in all the provinces in due time and I should like to know if there will not be a possibility of a misunderstanding as to the provincial branches of the Bank of Canada and the Provincial Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, June 22, consideration in committee of Bill No. 19, to incorporate the Bank of Canada-Mr. Rhodes -Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 25-Payment in gold.

The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) intended to move an amendment to this section which has been permitted to stand. He found it necessary to attend a committee this afternoon and has asked me to move his amendment. This section refers to the redemption of dominion notes in gold and as the hon. member and others with him do not believe in the gold basis or in having to redeem our dominion notes in gold, he has asked me to move:
That section 25 be amended by striking out subsection 1 and subsection 2.
Bank oj Canada

I should like to say a few words in support of the amendment which has just been moved. Subsection 1 imposes upon the bank the necessity of selling gold to any person who makes a demand therefor. The bank is compelled to redeem its notes in gold, to pay to anyone who presents sufficient notes approximately four hundred ounces of fine gold. I understand that there is no intention to compel the bank to redeem its notes in gold coin, but anyone outside of Canada who is able to secure sufficient Bank of Canada notes can go to the bank and demand gold. I think we are very foolish to impose this upon the bank when the preamble states that the purpose for which the bank is being set up is to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation. If this bank is to have a chance of doing that it seems to me that we should not impose upon it the necessity of redeeming its notes in gold. The terrific depression which has been upon us for the last few years is due chiefly to the financial deflation which occurred in the gold countries. Canada, being on the gold standard, had to follow the same financial policy and deflate her financial structure. Had we not been upon the gold standard and had we had an institution capable of managing credit and currency, such as I understand this Bank of Canada is to do, in my humble opinion the depression in Canada would not have affected us to one half the extent it has. Undoubtedly certain countries that have not been on the gold standard during the past four years are in a better position and their producers are in a better position because of this. For that reason I regret very much the present measure contemplates that the bank, the moment it is set up, is going to be under the liability of redeeming its notes in gold. It is true subclause 2 gives the governor in council power from time to time to suspend this subclause. But the bill as drafted makes it almost impossible for the bank to conduct its operations because it is faced with the necessity of redeeming its notes in gold. There is a distinct difference between compelling a bank to redeem its notes in gold as provided for in subclause 1 and having a gold reserve against notes. While at this time I am not opposing very strongly this clause which imposes upon the banks the necessity of carrying 25 per cent gold reserve for its notes, I think we are very unwise to have a clause inserted in the bill compelling the bank to redeem its notes in gold, because this places our whole price structure, our whole internal economy at the mercy of 
countries which are on the gold basis and which may at any time start deflation.
In a recent article in the Christian Science Monitor I notice an article stating that the Midland Bank and Gustav Cassel, one of the leading economists of Europe, agree on gold dispensability-that is, the ability to dispense with gold as a basis for currency. I do not at the moment suggest that we should dispense entirely with gold because I do not think the house would accept such an amendment, but I think we might leave out of this measure subclauses 1 and 2 of clause 25. Under clause 20, subclause 1, the bank has power to buy and sell gold and I think that is all that is necessary. Let us leave it to the bank to sell gold at whatever price they think is in the best interests of the nation. I hope the government will consider leaving it in the hands of the bank as to when they should buy and sell gold and at what price it should be sold, because under the clause with which we are at present dealing the bank will be under the liability of redeeming its notes in gold unless the government of the day sees fit to suspend this clause. It would be far better to leave it to the bank to decide at what price they will sell gold.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I shall not trespass upon the time of the committee at any length; I shall merely point out that subclause 2 provides of course for the present status being maintained, and it is not likely that until the other nations of the world have taken a forward step, the situation in this country will be other than it now is; that is, the condition prevailing in Great Britain and the United States will prevail here. But if we are going to have any form of stability in international exchange, it is quite obvious there must be some common yardstick for measurement, and apparently the only one that has presented itself for serious consideration so far is the gold standard because it has a universal value. I shall not amplify the matter because as it has been discussed so often, it would be very unfair to do so, but the notes are not to be exchanged now in terms of coinage as they were under the existing law. For instance, I can no longer get sovereigns in London. It is within the memory of most of us that in London the sovereign was a common coin to carry in one's pocket, with which one bought and sold goods and did one's business. It is no longer so because the only redemption you could make in London before the gold standard was suspended and after Mr. Churchill passed the law providing for the resumption of the gold standard was in terms of four hundred ounce gold bars.

Bank of Canada

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, you had to have $14,000 before you could get gold. That is the case in many countries in the world. It is called the bullion standard because gold coins are no longer necessary for the transaction of domestic business. You do not require $10 or $20 gold pieces to transact business in this country; it is only for external purposes that the gold standard is essential as providing a yardstick which is of universal length or a commodity which for a given quantity of it has a universal value, if I might use those words.
It will be observed that in this bill we have made some reference to the Bank for International Settlements. Canada has a small investment in that bank. It was felt that that bank might be of great service to all the countries of the world, and as a matter of fact it has been very useful. The 'president of it recently made this statement and I suppose, instead of going into this matter at length I might merely read his statement because it is put with much more authority than my observations would have. He says:
The gold standard is not an end in itself. It is a machinery and a medium for permitting facilitating and enhancing the exchange of goods, capital and services, internally and externally. Hence those who seek the reestablishment of a common standard are not seeking some fetish or intellectual abstraction, but are searching for the better economic welfare wli'ch inevitably flows from the increasing movement of goods, services and funds, which presupposes. in turn. some trustworthy menswp and medium of value and exchange to enable them to move. There should be no doubf about a general return to gold as the basis for the monetary system. The real question is whether definite steps will be adjourned for some time to come, or whether by common effort or as a result of the patent necessities disclosed by the failure of common effort an earlv attempt will be made to achieve a general settlement in the monetary and financial fields, thus leading the way to a restoration of the monetary system and to comnleting economic recovery.
The technioue of the gold standard requires and is capable of improvement in its domestic and in its international operation, particularly through the medium of continuous collaboration between the monetary authorities acting to the extent possible through a central agency. Collaboration may be an abstract noun, but it has proved in practice to he a concrete thing when central banks are faced with a specific problem in the financial or monetary field. The endeavoiir of the Bank for International Settlements shall be to contribute to the restoration of more orderly monetary and financial conditions in the international realm.
That is the position which we take in this new and young country in dealing with
problems that older countries have found can best be dealt with in the manner I have indicated. While in my judgment the gold standard is a sine qua non to the restoration of stabilized exchange, it is not an end in itself; it is merely the means by which the end is to be achieved. I trust the committee will realize, as the matter has been discussed so fully in the standing committee as well as in the house on several occasions, the summary which I have given from so eminent an authority as Mr. Fraser is much more valuable than any lengthy explanations that I might offer.

I do not wish to delay the committee, but I think hon. members might be interested in the first two paragraphs of the article to which I referred a moment or two ago; they put the matter in a much more concise way than I could do. This article is sent from London and the first paragraph reads:
The Midland Bank, one of Britain's "big five" banking institutions, and Professor Gustav Cassel. Swedish economist, have issued here two entirely independent statements, which, when taken in conjunction with one another constitute a scathing indictment of the theory still dear to old-fashioned bankers of the indispensability of the gold standard.
The Midland Bank finds that the almost universal resort to currency devaluation since the war has so changed world monetary conditions as to have dethroned gold as a stable measure of value. The conclusion is suggested that for practical purposes a currency off the gold standard is just as capable of being reliable as one that is on.
The concluding paragraph of the article reads:
The arguments of the Midland Bank and of Professor Cassel thus click with one another. The gold standard, the one says, has become unreliable. Germany, says the other, cannot recover until it frees its currency from impossible limitations which that standard has imposed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What year was that?

This is very recent, it was
in the Monitor just last week. In regard to the statement the Prime Minister read from the Bank for International Settlements, I think those who manage the Bank for International Settlements are interested in continuing the gold standard, because if they cannot the bank might have to undergo a great change if it is to continue as an institution. So perhaps they have an interest to serve. I am not saying that they are not sincere, but it may be that they are influenced by their own interest in making the statement they did in regard to returning to the gold standard. At any rate I think that a
425S
Bank of Canada

young country like Canada, with very great natural resources, a producer and exporter of primary products to the extent we are, would be foolish to contemplate a return to the gold standard under which our price level and our whole internal economy would be at the mercy of those who manage the world's monetary gold reserves.

I wish
to make just one observation in regard to the amendment moved by my hon. friend on the left. 1 think we must differentiate between the gold standard or gold exchange basis for international settlements and for our internal currency. I think the best economic opinion in the world in recent years, confirmed by various conferences, certainly by the English Macmillan committee, is that a gold basis is not required for internal currency. I do not think that even the twenty-five per cent coverage which was advocated last year by the British Empire section of the world monetary conference-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, by the whole conference.
Mr, MACKENZIE (Vancouver):-I do not believe it is necessary. I believe, in the words of the English Macmillan committee, quoting them just from memory, that the world should now gravitate towards a managed currency, managed by men of unchallenged independence. That in my opinion does not require a metallic basis as far as internal currency is concerned. The difficulty is to dissociate our internal currency from our credit in international transactions. Although I am personally and sentimentally in favour of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), I am afraid that the situation concerning it is just like that concerning our tariffs. I am in favour of reduced tariffs all over the world, but I recognize that it may be very difficult for us alone to reduce tariffs when all other nations are maintaining theirs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Good! At last!

We are discussing this in a very frank way. So in the same way I do not believe it is feasible for Canada at the present time to get away from gold as a standard of international exchange, although I do believe it is possible for Canada to abolish any metallic coverage whatsoever for her internal currency. The Prime Minister took me to task once when I used that argument; he said it was all a matter of confidence, that if we do away with metallic coverage for our internal currency, thereby

we lessen the confidence of other nations in our external credit. I think the proper conclusion is that gold as a basis for internal currency is only justifiable so far as it may assist that mistaken confidence which seems to be associated with gold by other nations of the world. I believe that the day is coming when gold will not be so highly valued as it is to-day as coverage for international currency. I believe that the national credit far transcends gold as a basis for the security of international currency. But I am not prepared at the present time to go the length of the hon. member who moved the amendment, although I do believe that in time gold coverage for internal currency will disappear.
Mr. 'COOTE: So that there may be no misunderstanding I would like to make it clear that I do not think there is any necessity for gold backing our internal currency. I think gold should be kept for the settlement of our international balances. What we object to is that this bank is to be put under the liability of selling gold at a fixed price to any person applying. That may have the effect at any time of hampering the bank, because too many of its notes may be presented for redemption in gold. I would point out that under section 21 it is provided that:
(1) The bank may
(a) buy and sell gold, silver, nickel and bronze coin and gold and silver bullion;
They have the power to sell gold. We are going to turn over to them all the gold. I think the bank should use that gold to the best advantage for the settlement of our international balances. It should be free to do that, but it should not be compelled to sell it at a fixed price. That would have the effect of placing our whole internal price level at the mercy of the gold-holding countries. That is what I object to, and that is why we are moving this amendment. We think gold should be used for the settlement of international balances, but we do not think that anyone who may be able to secure $14,000 of Bank of Canada note should be able to come and demand from the bank gold at a certain fixed price. We think that is too great a limitation to place upon the bank, if we intend that it should carry out the ideals laid down in the preamble of the bill. It may make it impossible for them to do the very thing that the bank is set up to do, that is to control credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation. They may have to control it in such a way as to conform to the gold policy of the United States and France, or the United States, France and Great

Bank of Canada
Britain. That is something that we should avoid. If we are to learn anything from the depression I think one lesson is that we cannot afford to place our internal price structure at the mercy of the gold countries. And we do it through section 25. It is true that the government can from time to time relieve the bank from the necessity of redeeming notes at all, but I say that as the section is drawn it makes the bank liable to redeem its notes in gold the very day it is set up. It seems to me that immediately the bank is set up and commences business the government would have to pass an order in council suspending subsection 1 of this section.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Just one word, because I should not like the hon. gentleman to leave a false impression on the mind of the committee. In the first place this country is not under the gold standard. Second, this section can only apply when the country is on the gold standard. Third, it will not be on the gold standard mVil other countries in the world have taken appropriate action in the same sense. Fourth, parliament will have to deal with the question of the value to be given to gold. At the present time the value fixed by statute is $20.67 an ounce, and until such time as parliament takes other action my hon. friend need not worry. There is no chance of any country or any syndicate accumulating notes of the bank and taking away the gold reserve of this country until such time as the nations of the world have arrived at some understanding with respect to the stability of exchange. How can I put the matter more clearly than to say that if a Canadian dollar has behind it 10 cents in gold and a Dutch guilder has behind it 96 cents in gold it is difficult to talk about the free exchange of goods until some stability has been arranged between the currencies of the two countries. And that applies to all the nations of the world. In my judgment the most essential matter to be dealt with at the moment to restore the world to its former prosperity is the stabilization of exchange;- perhaps not the most important but one of the most important of matters. I mention that because it is not intended that this section shall ever become operative until such time as the nations of the world take appropriate action.

Is it not true, at the same time, that if I have $14,000 or the equivalent in notes of the value of gold and decide to purchase a bar of 400 ounces of fine gold, I can get such gold in Bank of Canada notes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Quite so, in Bank of Canada notes.
Amendment lost on division.

Before the section carries I should like to ask another question, in regard to paragraph (c) of subsection (3) of section 25. My computation is that there will be about $63,000,000 of securities bearing interest at three per cent per annum, payable half yearly, which will be given as assets to the Bank of Canada on the day it opens for business. The section says:
to the amount of dominion notes outstanding on that day, except notes issued under the authority of the Finance Act.
I quite realize that we cannot make a computation for six months from now, but as at the present time what would be the amount of securities bearing interest at three per cent which would be given to the bank?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will recall what I said to the house the other day. The present law requires a gold coverage of twenty-five per cent on $50,000,000, which is $12,500,000 of gold. Under the statute of 1915 there were $26,000,000 of notes issued which, with the $12,500,000 totals $38,500,000.

That
$26,000,000 was covered by railway securities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows what they are. Taking the difference between $50,000,000 and $12,500,000, which is $37,500,000, with the $26,000,000, we have a total of $63,500,000 outstanding. Of course that will be increased by the enactment of the legislation I submitted to the house the other day, which contemplates an increase in the issue of dominion notes pending the coming into operation of this act.

Let us assume that the figure would be roughly $63,000,000 of securities bearing interest at three per cent. Roughly speaking the annual interest would amount to $1,800,000. How would that be charged? Would it be charged against the profits of the Bank of Canada or would it be paid out of the ordinary consolidated revenue fund?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Of course as a matter of bookkeeping the hon. gentleman realizes it will be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund, but will come back to the Dominion of Canada under this act.

But that should be charged against the bank before any dividends are paid. The taxpayer should not

Bank of Canada
be asked to pay an interest charge of $1,800,000. My own opinion is that the value of the securities will appreciate so rapidly that any charge of this kind should be a charge against the operations of the bank for that year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The question can only arise as a matter of bookkeeping, because unless the bank earned $225,000, which is a very small sum in view of the operations of the bank, I should think no directors would be disposed to pass the necessary resolution and no governor would be disposed to give it his approval unless the earnings were beyond the interest on the securities to which the hon. gentleman has referred. It is a matter about which we have had some discussion, but I think the hon. gentleman will realize that it would be rather difficult adequately to express the suggestion he has made in terms of a bill. I think we will have to depend largely upon the sound business sense of those in charge of the affairs of the bank who, I am sure, would not be disposed to pay four and a half per cent to the shareholders until such time as the earnings of the bank were equivalent to such sum exclusive of the matters to which my hon. friend has referred.

Then I have one further question. It should, perhaps, come up under section 30, but I might discuss it under paragraph (a) of subsection (3), which refers to gold held by the minister for redemption of dominion notes. Under this legislation we are transferring from the banks to the Bank of Canada $40,000,000 of gold, roughly speaking. Under section 30 there is a provision whereby the increased valuation may be given the banks in regard to an unspecified proportion of the $40,000,000 if the governor in council is satisfied that the said gold at the time of the transfer was being held by a chartered bank against liabilities elsewhere than in Canada. In such case the said profit is to belong to the chartered bank. We are taking the $40,000,000 from the chartered banks at the present valuation of $20.67 per ounce. An unstated proportion of that amount of gold will be reimbursed to the chartered banks at the present valuation if the governor in council is satisfied that this proportion is required for external obligations.
My point is this: I think it is practically an impossibility for the governor in council or any other body to determine what that percentage is going to be. I remember asking some of the bankers, in the committee on banking and commerce, if they could predetermine any definite percentage, and they said they could not do so. I think it places

a very dangerous responsibility upon any governor in council who happen to be in power to have to determine, by just one stroke of the pen, how much of the difference between $35 an ounce and $20.67 an ounce the chartered banks should receive as a result of a portion of their gold reserves being used for external obligations. I think in the interests of the governor in council, whoever they may be, this is a very far-reaching power, and the discretion might become dangerous. I do not know what the remedy is. The banks say they cannot decide; they say they need the whole $40,000,000 for external purposes. I do not agree with that for a moment, but I do submit that the Prime Minister is going to find it very difficult indeed, and possibly fraught with very grave consequences, to have to determine the amount of gold used for external obligations and the amount used for internal purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When we reach section 30 I will discuss that point.

I should like to ask a question with regard to subsections (1) and (2). When the act is declared will not this act override the order in council which now relieves the receiver general from the responsibility of redeeming notes in gold, and will a further order in council be passed immediately as provided for under subsection (2)?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Undoubtedly the hon. gentleman is quite correct. When the act is proclaimed, at the same time an order in council will be passed continuing the order in council now applying to dominion notes, under the provisions of this particular section.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 26-Reserves.

I have a few remarks to make in regard to subsection (4). At this time it is not my intention to cover all the ground that has been covered already with regard to silver, but I cannot allow this subsection to pass without comment while it includes the word "never". So I have an amendment to propose. I think it was generally understood on this side of the house the other evening that once the central bank is set up the initiative will come from the bank itself and not from the government. Here, in subsection 4, we have a mandatory clause which prohibits the bank from purchasing more than 1,671,802 ounces of silver in any year. I will send a copy of my amendment across to the Prime Minister. It is interesting to draw the attention of the committee to what transpired in July, 1933, at the London mone-

tary and economic conference. The question of gold and the practical return to gold came up at that time. The lead in connection with silver was taken by the United States and, as was stated by Senator King of the United States, upon his return they were side-tracked, and their resolution was gerrymandered and split in two.
At the present time the President of the United States is in my opinion making an attempt to redistribute gold. I have for my authority the words of Sir Arthur Salter who says in effect that that might be the effect of the United States purchasing so much silver. At the present time we have in Canada no gold coverage for domestic currency. As everyone knows, we have at the present time fiat money. It is true that probably a world agreement would be necessary before we could adopt bimetalism, and at the present time I am not advocating a return to bimetalism. At the monetary conference in London Canada agreed to purchase 1,671,802 ounces per year. The United States agreed to purchase 24,000,000 ounces per year, but she has now gone farther and has agreed to purchase up to 25 per cent of her monetary reserves, which will mean probably an increased purchase of one and a half to two billion ounces of silver. In spite of the covenant with the United States in this regard we are placing in this bill a mandatory clause saying that the bank shall never purchase more than our allotment agreed to in London. Personally I think this is a slap in the face so far as the United States is concerned.
I am not asking that we should go on to bimetalism at the present time. We took a step in the right direction when we agreed to purchase over one million ounces yearly, but to prohibit the banks from purchasing more is a slap in the face so far as the United States is concerned. We are saying to that country, "You can do what you like about your monetary affairs and your plan to distribute gold." I would ask the Prime Minister this question:	How is it possible to
redistribute the present gold reserves of the world? No one can tell. No economist or financier can tel! how the stock of gold, three-quarters of the world's supply of which is held by France and the United States, can again be redistributed. It is the consensus of opinion of those who have studied the matter that President Roosevelt is at least making some effort towards this end, and it may be that through his efforts gold will again be redistributed. We could very well use silver in this country as coverage for our domestic uses. No country would stand
Bank oj Canada
to gain more than Canada by such a use of silver. We produce annually between 18,000,000 and 24,000,000 ounces of silver. In the late years the price has been too low to further the production of silver, but if it goes to sixty cents an ounce, as it shows every likelihood of doing, the industry will give employment to thousands of citizens, and especially would that be true in British Columbia.
I think the Prime Minister should consider taking out the word "never"; it should not be there. It is not fair to have that word in the act. The amendment which I have sent to you, Mr. Chairman, would make the clause read as follows:
The bank shall during the years 1935, 1936 and 1937 purchase and hold of newly-mined Canadian silver, as agreed to by Canada at the London monetary and economic conference, all such silver as the minister shall require.
I think that is a fair amendment. It is not mandatory and at least it carries out the agreement made at the conference. If the government were so minded instructions could be issued to the bank to purchase more silver.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
makes the mistake which is not unusual even to those who have given as much study as he has to this matter. He is confusing the bank with the government. The United States government is doing the purchasing of silver. There is nothing in this legislation to prevent our government from buying silver. This bill deals only with the bank. If the hon. gentleman would take the trouble to differentiate between the two he would not have made the error he has now made.
When the other day I introduced the bill dealing with the issue of dominion notes I pointed out that we proposed to buy in the year 1934 a supply of silver in the manner indicated in that measure. For the years 1935, 1936 and 1937 we have placed the responsibility for the purchase of it upon the central bank. As the bank succeeds to the custody of the gold and silver now held by the government, and I may7 point out that we have five or six years' silver now in hand for ordinary monetary purposes, we did not feel we would be fair to the bank if we required it to purchase beyond 1,671,802 fine ounces in any of the years I have indicated. If, as a matter of national policy, the government decides to buy silver, as congress has authorized the president to do, that is a matter for the future. The purchases, I should think it is only fair to say, will proceed in the United States by the government of the United States. The total
Bank of Canada

purchases under the proposals before congress would amount to something less than 1,700,000,000 ounces. But the whole situation in connection with silver turns not upon the action of the government of the United States nor of the government of Canada. India holds the key to the silver situation. This is a matter which was discussed at some length in London and the agreement arrived at was not easy of conclusion. It represents the best arrangement the nations of the world were prepared to make, having regard to the conditions with respect to silver and the very large quantities of silver held by India. Those quantities are administered, really, by one commissioner, and are tremendous. They are so great that if the price of silver were to rise, as has been suggested, the effort to sell on the part of India would be so great as inevitably to produce a very great reduction in the price.
I think I am right when I say that India has agreed to sell not more than so many million ounces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Under this agreement;
that is the reason it is here.
She has agreed not to sell it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

And in regard to the stocks
held in Canada, it is a matter of comment, and rather strange that we hold the smallest stock of silver. Our whole stock amounts to only 2,000,000 ounces. That is all that the stock of silver in Canada amounts to, despite the fact that we are the third largest silver producing country in the world. Yet we are holding only one year's agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: One what?

The information given me is
at the present time we are holding 2,254,000 ounces of silver, and that the silver we have been using during the past three years has come from worn out coins. We have taken the pure silver from the worn out coins, after melting them down, and have debased them from 900 to 800 fine. Why was the word "never" put in the clause? Why was such a restriction put in there, in order to keep the bank from purchasing more silver?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The word "never" is
probably an undesirable word to use in a statute, but it was put in this bill for a definite purpose, namely to prevent false hopes being created in the hearts of those who might be concerned. During the currency of the world's agreement it will be observed by the hon. gentleman that everything depends upon the agree-
ment being kept. And India, being the key to the situation and having agreed as she did agree, we have added these words to indicate what our position will be, because we will have more silver than we will know just what to do with. That is the position. We have
2,000,000 ounces now, and we are buying substantially about 1,700,000 ounces a year. We have transferred that obligation to the bank. That is for the reason that we cannot contemplate this bank loading itself up with that silver. The government might do it; we might pass a statute to do it, but we are not going to place the bank in that false position. It will be observed that the legislation does not contemplate the central reserve bank buying the silver; it is the government that buys it; and if this parliament in its wisdom desires at a later date to pass a statute providing for the government purchasing silver, this will not stand in the way of it. If the time ever comes when the word "never" should be removed in respect to the bank, of course it will be a simple thing to do that.
