On section 27-Reserve to be maintained by chartered banks.

There is an important amendment in subsection 1 of section 27. As originally brought down the section, then numbered 26, provided:
Every chartered bank shall on and after the day when the bank is authorized to commence business, maintain deposits with the bank which shall always be equal to five per centum of its deposit liabilities within Canada.
Subsection 1 of section 27 now reads:
Every chartered bank shall on and after the day on which the bank is authorized to commence business maintain a reserve of not less than five per centum of its deposit liabilities within Canada ...
The words to which I wish to call attention particularly are the following, which appear in italics:
... and such reserve consist of a deposit with the bank and of notes of the bank held by such bank.
The change made would allow the five per cent to be composed partly of notes of the Bank of Canada held by the chartered banks and the balance held on deposit. It seems to me that if there is any necessity of requiring the chartered banks to hold a deposit with the Bank of Canada, the central bank, certainly five per cent is small enough, and I submit that this change that has been made in the bill is in a sense destroying the value

Bank oj Canada
of the section. It is through the operation of this subsection, or partly through it, that the central bank can control to some extent the amount of credit issued. It is one of those measures which give the central bank control.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. member explain how the chartered banks could thus control credit?

When the chartered banks are extending credit, because of that they increase their deposits and as their deposit liabilities increase-their own liabilities-'they must increase their deposit with the central bank. I do not know what amount of notes the banks will carry, but after their own note issue privilege is practically discontinued, after a period of years, they might carry practically the whole of the five per cent in notes of the Bank of Canada. I think the change made weakens the position of the central bank, and that the original provision which required the chartered banks to carry five per cent on deposit is not too much. In order to bring the matter properly before the committee I move that section 27 be amended by striking out subsection 1 and substituting therefor the following:
Every chartered bank shall on and after the day when the bank is authorized to commence business, maintain deposits with the bank of not less than five per centum of its deposit liabilities within Canada.
Some students with whom I have discussed the matter think that five per cent is too small, that the banks might be required to carry even more than that. I do not think the bill as it stood originally required too large a deposit from the chartered banks. The present provision is really not adequate and I think we ought to substitute for it the section contained in the original bill.

I
thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Macleod. He may recall that I drew the attention of the banking and commerce committee to this very section, and the protest I made was that it was moved practically at the eleventh hour of the proceedings of the committee, and without notice. We are all aware that the chartered banks were very much opposed to this provision for a five per cent deposit. It is a matter of judgment as between two principles, which are these. The first question is: Does the Bank of Canada require a five per cent deposit from the chartered banks of Canada for its proper and adequate functioning? The second question is: Will the deposit of five per cent work such an injury on any one of the chartered
banks that it cannot function or carry on? I am rather inclined to agree with the hon. member, that the Bank of Canada will need a five per cent deposit from the chartered banks to enable it to function as it should. On the other hand, my information has been that in the case of one or two of the chartered banks the section as previously worded might work a very distinct hardship, and in considering the proposed amendment it is a matter of judgment as between these two principles. Personally I am in favour of the amendment. I believe the banks can deposit their five per cent without taking into consideration notes of the Bank of Canada, which will be in the various tills of the chartered banks as they continue to operate and function.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The provisions of the
section to which the hon. member for Macleod has directed attention are of course very important. May I point out that this section compels the banks of Canada to deposit with the central bank, as the hon. gentleman says, approximately five per cent of their deposit liabilities.

One
hundred millions altogether.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That means that the
banks in Canada will pay into the central bank about one hundred million dollars. That money may represent in part money on which they are paying interest. They are getting nothing for it; they get no interest on this one hundred millions, which is held by the central bank as a depository for the reserve liability of the chartered banks. When the matter came under consideration by the minister, on the state of facts disclosed from an examination of the returns, it was found that the chartered banks of Canada had been maintaining large quantities of money as till money, that is, bank notes which were held in their vaults but which were not in use- their own notes which were not in use until such time as they were put across the counter. The till money of some of the banks amounted to as high as 815,000,000. The law requires the banks to hold forty per cent of whatever cash reserves they have in Dominion of Canada bills. The other day on inquiry I found that one of the chartered banks had $40,000,000 of Dominion of Canada notes; another had, if I remember correctly, $38,000,000; and-I speak subject to correction- another had $21,000,000. It has always been of the utmost importance, so far as we are concerned, that the position of the chartered banks with relation to Dominion of Canada
Bank oj Canada

notes should be such as would ensure the circulation of this form of national credit. I will put it that way. Confronted with this situation the banks say:	No other central
bank bill undertook to impose upon us an absolute percentage which we had to maintain. They contended that in this country there had been averages which indicated that five per cent was reasonable. They do not complain of that but they say: If you put us in default if we drop below five per cent for a day, it will have a very serious effect upon our general position. Therefore, we have arrived at the conclusion which is indicated in this bill by which five per cent is to be maintained by the banks in Bank of Canada notes as a reserve for their deposits, but part of that money is to be on deposit with the central bank as a working balance which they may change from day to day by additions and deductions and by deposits and cheques against the balance. This is a great convenience to the banks and it cannot be said to be detrimental to this country at the moment. It enables a condition which is new to this country to be met by a method which will not be harmful to the principle or be a serious departure from the principle that the reserves of the chartered banks shall be held in deposits in the central bank or by the notes of the central bank. The regulations will take proper care of this situation. I quite appreciate the criticism made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) but it must not be forgotten that the banks feel that this section added to the provisions of another section treats them very cruelly. I think this is an accommodation to meet the difficulties and they will not have the same complaint as they previously had in connection with the unfair treatment accorded by this bill.
Does the Prime Minister feel the section as now drawn gives ample security to the Bank of Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am satisfied that for
the transition period between the old and new regime, it will be ample. I might say to the hon. gentleman who is a Scotchman that the chartered banks of England maintain about ten or ten and a half per cent but it may amaze him to know that on the average the holdings are only six per cent of Bank of England notes, the balance being on deposit with the Bank of England. It seems to me that we are meeting the situation in the way which the larger experience of Great Britain has enabled them to meet a similar situation.

The banks must hold some forty per cent of their reserve in dominion notes but I do not believe there is anything in the Bank Act to say what that reserve should be. Do I understand that the five per cent which the banks must have with the Bank of Canada or in their tills must be in Bank of Canada notes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. As the hon. gentleman will note from the section there will be a determination by the banks from time to time. The banks may buy notes and hold them apart from what is held in their tills, but the deposits they will have to make will be deposits in ordinary business. They must have working balances and they cannot have working balances unless there are accretions of fresh deposits to meet withdrawals. They must have working balances to meet the varied demands of business from day to day.
Just like deposits under the Bank Act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Exactly, over and above the minimum. In matters of this kind it has been found in practice that the working balances and the deposits are usually well above the statutory minimum.

Would the amount of
dominion notes now carried by the banks be more than five per cent of their deposit liabilities? If that is so we are really not compelling them to hold any greater reserve than what they hold at the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The figures for April 30, 1934, show the dominion notes held by all banks a-s totalling $128,540,497 against assets of $2,831,000 000 and total deposits of about
82.000.000.000. The latter figure is not given in a separate column and it would be necessary to add the four columns.
At any rate their holding of dominion notes is more than five per cent of the deposits?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Slightly more.

I take it that most of the Dominion notes now held by the banks are in the form of large legals which are used for settling accounts between themselves. Under this bill they will not use those but will simply give cheques on the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I thank the hon. gentleman for directing attention to that fact. A great proportion of the Dominion of Canada notes held by the banks is not a medium of circulation, it consists of counters for the purpose of making transactions between the banks through the clearing house.

Bank of Canada
In large denominations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As a matter of fact they are just counters of 850,000 or 8100,000. In view of the fact that this bill contemplates the steady diminution of the power of issue by the chartered banks and the placing in circulation of increasing quantities of Bank of Canada notes, I think the hon. gentleman will see that in practice it will work out much more satisfactorily for credit purposes.

I have listened with a great deal of attention to what was said by hon. members who have spoken and by the Prime Minister himself. I have received the impression that this is an academic debate on banking as everyone has spoken about the theory of banking. This section refers to the deposit liabilities of the chartered banks. If hon. members will look at the reports published monthly in the Canada Gazette they will see that the deposits in the chartered banks have been increasing since 1930. There is no lack of money, in fact there is more than there was in 1930. The trouble is the lack of circulation of that money. People who have money in the banks keep it there. They feel secure and they will not invest it in different concerns. The confidence of this country has not been restored and people are still keeping their deposits in the banks. What is needed now is the circulation of money; the people should be taught to put their money to other uses and to invest it in order to give wrnrk to people. There is a phrase used in a drama known to many hon. members to the effect that business is other people's money. I cannot find anything in this bill which will increase the circulation of money. The role of this central bank should be to activate the circulation of money. It should be like a policeman trying to get people to move on in a jammed street. I cannot find that this bill is going to do that, and I cannot see what use it will be. It is simply another complication; it is simply some more legislation, the same as the amalgamation of railways which is coming shortly. There is amalgamation of everything; everything is centralized and I do not see the use of this bill if it is not to activate the circulation of money which is deposited in huge quantities in the chartered banks of Canada. Trade can be restored and money will circulate when there is more confidence throughout this country, but as long as people are afraid to make any investments the money will stay in the banks and there will be no improvement of trade. Therefore this legislation should be considered from not only a
theoretical but a practical point of view. This is the main point. What is the use of having immense numbers, libraries, of statute books? What does this mean to tire common people? They want work and to be paid for the work they do. They want the money to go around from one to another and come to the banks in smaller deposits. When this is done it will be a great benefit to the country, but I do not see anything practical in this bill.

I should like to say a word with regard to one of the points brought forward by my hon. friend. I am not at all agreeing with his general statement. There is a tremendous possibility in this legislation for expansion of credit. In the first place it will take over the gold held by the Minister of Finance for redemption of dominion notes and amounting to about
870,000,000. The appreciated value of this as taken over by this legislation will amount to about $117,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Roughly S120,000,000.

In the
second place, we are taking over that portion of the chartered banks' gold which is not required for external obligations, and that will amount to another S60,000,000, so that provided the present value keeps up, the bank will have a gold value of about $177,000,000. Under the flexible provision of twenty-five per cent metallic coverage, one can imagine the power for expansion given thereby. We did not have any such power under the previous legislation, even under the Finance Act.

I admire the learning of
the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, but it is not illuminating. I know no more now than I did before and I have been listening to him very carefully. He speaks about a tremendous value of millions of dollars and all that sort of thing. That is not the point; it is that a man should have an opportunity to be paid for some work at three, four or five dollars a day. That would mean more for him than hearing about millions of dollars. My hon. friend spoke in a very learned manner and I am always pleased to listen to him, but as I said, I know no more now than I did before he spoke.

On section 30-Disposition of profits from sales.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Vancouver Centre has directed attention to the difficulty that will arise in making a division under this clause of profits resulting from the sale by the bank of gold coin and bullion transferred to it pursuant to the provisions of clauses 25 and 28. I do not for a single minute minimize the difficulty, but to state in this bill an exact figure would be unfair to this bank as it would be unfair to the chartered banks. Some of the banks have external liabilities that are still liabilities in terms of gold. The banks have some foreign liabilities which it is unnecessary to say to this committee have, by the action of the legislatures of those countries, no longer to be met in terms of gold. For instance, the decision of the House of Lords in one case greatly increases the liabilities as it was indicated by a decision of the court of appeal when we were discussing the matter here in the early months of the year. The question whether certain liabilities in the United States in terms of securities are to be met in a particular way or by what would be the equivalent of the value of the gold at the time is still unsettled. Then of course we do not disguise the fact that we have in this country a few questions in that regard that are not yet settled, for instance in connection with some few people who in 1933 declined to accept other payment of their bonds that fell due and demanded that they should be paid in gold. There are very few of them, but now and then we have seen such cases in the newspapers; the amount is not largo. That, however, does not touch the external side of the matter. I appreciate that this places upon the governor in council a substantial responsibility, but it is one that must be taken with respect to many of these matters. I should say, speaking antecedent to the occasion arising, it must be the subject matter of discussion, agreement and arrangement based upon such expert knowledge applied to the facts as will enable a reasonable disposition to be made of the matter in the light of the monetary value attaching to the external liabilities in terms of gold. That is all that can reasonably be said about the matter.

This
places a tremendous responsibility upon the governor in council. I would suggest the insertion of some provision such as "upon report by the deputy minister" or "upon report by the inspector general," to get somebody responsible for the disposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No action on such a
clause as this is taken by council except on a report of the Minister of Finance, and usually it has been the custom, grown up in recent years, that the Minister of Finance makes the submission and he says that this course is recommended by-indicating, as the hon. gentleman has said, the deputy minister and sometimes others as well. I can assure the hon. member that so far as the present governor in council is concerned, the responsibility will not be lightly exercised or too readily undertaken without having clear knowledge of what is involved as a result of it.

Before the preamble passes I wish to move an amendment. I appreciate that the preamble as it stands is nearly allembracing, but not quite. It is drawn with considerable care but I do not think it fully covers our needs. I wish to remind the committee that since the war we have paid out, I think, about 81,900,000,000 in interest in this country; our interest burden has increased eleven times during the last twenty years. For that reason I wish to move the following amendment to the preamble:
That the preamble of Bill No. 19 be amended by inserting after the word "Canada" in the second line the words: "to make use of the national credit at cost and."
The preamble will then read as follows:
Whereas it is desirable to establish a central bank in Canada to make use of the national credit at cost and to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation, to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment, so far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action, and generally to promote the economic and financial welfare of the Dominion: Therefore, His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
I trust the committee will give this their best consideration, as it is in the best interests of Canada.

Dominion Notes Act

Mr. Chairman, before you submit this amendment, may I say that while those debts are spoken of only as liabilities, in fact they are also assets. As has already been said here, if the Dominion of Canada owes $2,500,000,000 that is its national debt, but that debt is an asset of those who hold Canadian bonds; therefore it must be considered in both aspects. When we speak of the debt we must have in mind also that the bonds representing it are assets of the people who hold them and constitute a large part of the wealth of this country. The matter must not be considered from the passive angle only, but also from the active. I shall not enlarge any further upon it; I merely wish to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that in this matter there is on one side a debtor and on the other side a creditor. Large amounts of Canadian bonds, national, provincial and municipal, are held by Canadians, and they are the wealth of those people, who live on the income derived from them. The matter must be considered from that angle as well.

The
second section of the bill provides for repeal of the Dominion Notes Act on a day to be proclaimed, and the first section for repeal of section 5 of the old Dominion Notes Act, which provided for a note issue of $50,000,000, and increases the amount to $120,000,-
000.	It is not necessary to add much to the
very comprehensive review of the dominion notes situation given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) the other day. Briefly, before confederation the provinces of Canada then in existence had their several note issues. These were taken over by the dominion authority in 1867. The principle underlying our dominion note issue and also those of the provinces was that there should be a partial gold coverage up to a certain amount, and beyond that limit the coverage should be ons hundred cents on the dollar. The other day the Prime Minister referred to the fact that under this legislation there would be a possible total note issue of $223,000,000 odd. I presume that was made up as follows: Total notes $120,000,000; twenty-five per cent of gold $30,000,000, and the total gold left of the $117,000,000 at the appreciated valuation, $87,000,000 odd; this would be $120,000,000 plus $87,000,000, or $207,000,000, and with the $16,000,000 odd already covered by securities makes the total of $223,000,000.
Speaking for myself, I am pleased indeed that the Prime Minister has introduced this legislation. I can only regret that it was not introduced over three years ago. Hon. gentlemen opposite may recall that at least a few of us on this side did advocate three or four years ago the introduction of precisely such legislation. They may recall that when the Dominion Notes Act was passed in the first place the amount issued was not $50,000,000 but $30,000,000, which was subsequently increased to $50,000,000 and in 1915 by a further $26,000,000. In two years there was a total increase in the note issue of Canada of $46,000,000. Now under this legislation according to the Prime Minister there is a possible increase of $52,000,000 odd, the difference between the present note issue of $171,000,000 and what he calls the possible note issue under this legislation, of $223,000,000. I do not agree exactly with the Prime Minister that this legislation is made possible by the appreciation in the value of gold. According to his own, figures, taking our present Finance Act, $69,000,000 in gold at a valuation of $20.67 an ounce would give a coverage of thirty-one per cent even for the contingent note issue of $223,000,000. In my judgment thirty-one per cent is more than ample to cover our internal note issue circulation. I think twenty-five per cent was fixed last year as a sufficient coverage. Under the increased valuation of the Finance Act, according to the figures given the other day the gold which will then be available during the transition period before the Bank of Canada commences business will be 52J per cent of this note issue of $223,000,000. My
426S
Dominion Notes Act

only complaint in that regard, Mr. Chairman, is that the increase should be far greater than it is. Instead of increasing it from $50,000,000 to 8120,000,000 I think on any scientific basis the Prime Minister or any government would be entitled to increase the note issue of Canada to-day much more than is being done at the present time. I think an increase of 8100,000,000 or more would be absolutely justified. I recall that three or four years ago the English Macmillan committee established a different scientific basis. They said it was a safe basis for any nation to issue notes to the extent of one-fifth the total bank deposits, which in Canada would result in a note issue of about $400,000,000 as against 8171,000,000 at the present time. On the other hand I think that when the Bank of Canada is constituted, with its more elastic and flexible provisions, with the appreciated gold taken from the banks and from the Finance department totalling perhaps 8177,000,000, the note issue powers of the bank are going to be simply tremendous.
I am not criticizing the details of this bill; I am criticizing two particulars of it. In the first place I am complaining because this was not done three or four years ago, and my second complaint is that the note issue is not more substantial. With regard to financing public works by the issue of credit, I am entirely in favour of that so long as that issue of credit is made on the basis of security, so long as it is not uncontrolled inflation. The Prime Minister mentioned the appreciated value of gold, and he also mentioned the resolution of the London conference of last year. In my judgment neither of these arguments is required to justify this present legislation.
Another submission I want to make to the right hon. gentleman is this: When we come to receive the appreciated value of the gold which we are taking over from the banks we should consider that an asset which belongs to the .people of Canada. It should not be used for the temporary financing of public works or anything of the kind; it should be used only for the reduction of our national debt. I am in favour of these two principles, first applying the appreciation in the value of gold to the reduction of the national debt, and second the principle of financing public works by the direct issue of currency instead of placing great interest obligations upon our shoulders for years to come. With these reservations, Mr. Chairman, I want to commend the legislation introduced by the Prime Minister.

I have always been greatly interested in this question of note issue or, as we sometimes call it, controlled inflation. I have never been able to get at the bottom of the difference between the advocacy of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) and that of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), and the present attitude of the government. Until last year the hon. member for Macleod advocated inflation without the significant word " controlled " before it, according to my memory. The 'hon. member for Vancouver Centre seemed to want it about what it is in this bill-a certain measure of controlled inflation. As a beginner in these matters economic and financial I want to know why the government can do this thing now. with the apparent approval of almost everyone, when the government could not do it when we needed it so badly, three years ago.
The economic conference seems to have given its O.K. to this. What had they to do with our business? Could we not have done it without 'waiting these interminable two or three years? As a farmer I know what it meant to us two or three years ago and less in promoting low farm prices. I do not pretend to be any authority on monetary matters, but I know what hurts and what does not hurt, what helps and what does not help the farmer to get a proper price for his product. Without knowing a. quarter as much as he does I feel as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre feels, but I want to know why this measure was delayed so long and why we had to wait until the economic conference told us to go ahead. This is about the only thing they did tell us, so far as I recall, except the wheat agreement, which is not much good, if any. Why did we wait so long, and what circumstances prevail now which justify this measure to-day but which did not justify it previously? That is what I should like to get at.

Since the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) has mentioned my name I must say, almost as a matter of privilege, that I have never, in this house or any other place, advocated uncontrolled inflation.
You did not mention "uncontrolled."
I should like to make that very plain. If the hon. gentleman doubts that he can look at any speech I have made in this house.

I do not want to do my hon. friend any injustice at all, because

Dominion Notes Act
I think he was the pioneer in advocating inflation. But I never detected the word "controlled" in his remarks, though last year he went out of his way to shove it right to the front. If I am wrong I should be delighted to have my hon. friend correct me.

If the hon. gentleman would do me the honour of reading the first speech on the subject I made in this house he would see that the word "inflation" does not occur in it at all. I protested against the deflation which has taken place, and I suggested that Canada should abandon the gold standard and allow her dollar to depreciate in outside countries. In other words I suggested that we should devalue our dollar, and I should like to make that plain. I have never advocated uncontrolled inflation; I believe in controlling the economic forces that we use in our daily life. When I protest against deflation someone always reads into my remarks that I want uncontrolled inflation. Of course I have been accused of wanting to use the printing press, but I suggest that this is what the Prime Minister is going to do. He is going to print more dominion notes with practically the same amount of gold we have had in the treasury for the last few years. We might as well have had these notes printed three or four years ago; we might even have had a few more. It would not have been more dangerous then than it is now, and it would have been a great deal of help. That 840,000,000 might have been working all these years at the increased velocity suggested this afternoon by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), because unfortunately in studying economics we find that when the quantity of money is reduced the velocity of its circulation always slows down.

Since my name has been mentioned I should like to ask the hon. gentleman a question. He has said that he favours controlled inflation. Would he be good enough to tell the house what is the limit of controlled inflation?

At the moment I was not
even advocating controlled inflation. I would suggest to the hon. member that what we are getting now is a little bit of inflation. The quantity of money which is moving about and serving the public is greatly restricted, and I congratulate the Prime Minister on taking this step to put more money into circulation. I want to congratulate the Prime Minister for using this money to construct public works in order to provide employment, instead of giving people the dole. May I say that I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre when 74726-270
he says this measure is several years late. We are now in the fourth year of deflation, and we should have taken steps of this kind long ago, though it is better late than never. This is a very feeble, short step. As I remember it, speaking from memory and using approximate figures, the gold held by the government itself is in the neighbourhood of
870,000,000. Using the very basis which the Prime Minister says was suggested by the world conference as quite adequate, the twenty-five per cent gold reserve, we could issue $280,000,000 of dominion notes. That would be quite safe and quite in keeping with the canons of sound finance, whatever that may be. I understand we have about $170,000,000 in dominion notes now outstanding, so we might safely issue another $110,000,000. If we are going to issue $40,000,000, and if we have decided it is quite proper to adopt this new basis of gold coverage, I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister that he could go at least to the extent of $100,000,000. May I also point out to the house that gold now commands a much higher value. I think it is about seventy per cent higher than it is valued under our currency act. So we could increase by seventy per cent the gold basis for the issue of notes, which would bring the amount of gold at the new valuation to about $119,000,000. And if you used that as a basis for an issue with twenty-five per cent gold coverage you could issue notes up to $470,000,000, and still be financially sound.

How would you control
your coincident increase in credit which naturally follows from putting this much into circulation?

Control it through the central bank. If the central bank is given adequate powers it could control the situation. As I suggested this afternoon, the reserves which the banks must carry are not sufficient. The central bank could easily control if we gave it the power to require the chartered banks to carry with it a certain percentage of their deposit liabilities, as a deposit in the central bank, give the central bank power to vary the percentage of such deposit and they can prevent too great inflation of bank credit. At the moment there is no danger of that, because there are not enough people whose credit is good who will assume the responsibility of borrowing from the bank. So we are not liable to have any inflation of bank credit from that.
I do not wish to speak at length, except to say that I believe the Prime Minister is taking a step in the right direction and that I regret

Dominion Notes Act

he has not gone farther. I suggest that he should go farther. I am not suggesting that he must go as far as is possible under the new valuation of gold, but let us have enough of these dominion notes issued to finance a worth while program of public works. Public works may be considered as an asset and not a liability, and they are a very good asset on which we could issue new money. That is, there is an asset which justifies the issue of new money, as well as having twenty-five per cent gold reserve behind it. But so far as the other seventy-five per cent is concerned, we would have useful public works behind it, and I believe that would be a very good basis on which to issue money.
I am very glad the Prime Minister has taken this step, but I should be pleased if before the legislation is finally passed he would consent to go a little farther.

Before the Prime Minister answers I should like to state some of my dilemmas. It was always contended two or three years ago that by issuing these additional notes with the same coverage we would have given that much more currency to put into circulation for business requirements-not for a building program, but just so that we might have it available so that any of us might get it for the ordinary running of our businesses. I never could see that. I have no brief for the Prime Minister. It was, I repeat, a matter of issuing such additional notes so that notes would be available for all and sundry businesses, when there was all kinds of money already available in the banks. It certainly was not a question of the availability of larger amounts of currency in order to do a larger business. The money was there in abundance in the bank all the time. We did not need any more currency then to do our business. It needed even less currency then because there was less business being done; therefore less currency would have been sufficient. The banks were filled with currency waiting for investment, and waiting to make loans where they could obtain what they considered proper security. Why is it needed now? Why has the conference to tell us when to do it? This is all a great mystery to me, and I am sure the Prime Minister will do some unravelling in connection with this enigma, and will throw some new light upon it. I know there is a difference between ordinary currency and an investment in public works. What this new note issue really does is to get away from going on the market and borrowing money.

It averts borrowing more money, and increasing our national debt. If we did not do this as outlined in the bill we would have to borrow money abroad; we would have to add to our national debt, an objectionable procedure just now and one which should be avoided if possible. If there is anything in the suggestion that this is just being done now before an election I must say that would be a most unworthy purpose.
What is the limit of controlled inflation? No answer.

I should like to say that
although I intended to, I did not answer the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). He asked my opinion as to where we would stop controlled inflation, or how far it should go. The determining factor in that case would be the average commodity price level in Canada. I think that is generally agreed upon by economists as being the factor which determines when the controlled inflation should stop. There should be no further inflation after we get to a certain agreed price level. That point would be agreed upon before a policy was commenced. I believe that is what the central bank may do. They should set, as their objective, a certain commodity price level. We have chosen the price level of 1926. We would take the index price of all commodities in that year, the index figure representing the average commodity price. Let us have a policy of controlled inflation or reflation-and I believe the latter is a much better word-let us raise the index figures of commodity prices to a point as near as possible to the figures obtaining in 1926. That would make it possible for producers to meet their liabilities. But while the price level is perhaps only sixty per cent of what it was when we incurred debts in 1926, we have to produce forty per cent more commodities to get the same amount of money to pay our debts. When we produce the extra forty per cent-and if we do succeed in doing so-then we drive the price level down because we have overproduced. We must have a certain price for our products, if we are going to meet our liabilities. The hon. member for Temiscouata says that our bonds are not only liabilities, that they are assets. They are assets only if those who must pay taxes out of which this interest comes, can meet their payments. If the price levels go too low, that becomes impossible for the producers, and when enough producers get into that position the interest on the bonds cannot be met, except from new borrowings, a condition which cannot go on indefinitely.

Dominion Notes Act
So I say the matter of getting a certain price level for producers is a fundamental matter for this house to determine when we are discussing monetary policies.
I think the Prime Minister will agree with me as to the importance of having a certain price level for our products, and if it is necessary for our producers it is necessary for Canada to have it so that the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities may meet their liabilities. The interest can be paid only out of production. If the price of our products goes too low the payment of interest becomes impossible-just as impossible as taking four gallons of water out of a one gallon can. It is for that reason that for the last three or four years I have urged monetary action to raise price levels.

I had asked certain questions of the government, and the answer came from the hon. member for Macleod after he had said that he did not desire to reply to my question.

I said that I intended to answer it but I forgot, and that is why I rose to make reply. I did not wish to interrupt (he Prime Minister.

I am not saying that at all. What I am saying is that when I asked the question of the hon. member for Macleod he said that he was not discussing the matter at the moment, but he did not tell me that he would be good enough to rise afterwards and give a lengthy explanation of the matter. Now I am a layman; I am not a banker. I have here a dollar bill and if through inflation it were converted into a two dollar bill or a three dollar bill it would mean that instead of one dollar I should have three dollars. But if the increase were general the result would be that I would not be able to buy any more with that three dollars than I can with this dollar bill. Therefore what is the use of inflation? I remember well that last year, during a debate on the very same subject, I asked the hon. member for Macleod some questions along the same lines. I asked him: If we have normal trade what is the use of inflation? I have not the text of his answer but I remember distinctly what he said; he said that if trade were normal, if we had the same trade now that we had in 1930 there would be no necessity for inflation. He said it twice, and the third time I asked the same question and he told me that if he had said it previously it was because he had not properly understood what I had asked him before.
Now, I do not see what relation there can be between the central bank and the average figured value of goods. I do not see how the Bank of Canada can increase the price of butter from twenty cents, as it is now, to fifty or sixty cents as was promised before the election. I do not see how the Bank of Canada can do that, but if my hon. friend can explain it to me I should like him to explain it in very plain language which can be understood by a layman like myself. I am not a banker as he is. I am not a technician; but I do not believe in all this artificial, superficial, fictitious business. There must be something real; there must be something that exists not only in the imagination but in reality. Consider all that has been inspired by the economists who have written books upon books to describe their dreams. First of all, we remember Plato who lived a long time ago. He described the ideal city. Walking with other philosophers he described his dreams, and he gave them to us in books that are immortal. But the ideal city as seen by Plato in one of his dreams has never existed in reality. And now we have all sorts of economists who are preaching cures for every national trouble. They are writing books. Some of them live in England some in the United States, and others in France and Ger-
Dominion Notes Act

many; and here in this House of Commons we have listened to the opinions of Sir Arthur Salter and of Schacht, the president of the Reichsbank. All these people have beautiful theories which will make everyone rich. Well, they may be sincere, but they are not serious, and these experiments cannot be carried on on any large scale. Take a chemist like Pasteur; take a man like Claude Bernard; take Lord Lister. These men confined their experiments within a narrow field. They tried first to discover the truth by experimenting on a very small scale and then, when they saw that that limited experiment was successful, they extended it and carried it on on a larger scale. This I submit is what should be done. It is very dangerous to venture into the unknown on the word of men who, though they may be scientists or men with keen legal minds, have no practical experience. I am sure, for instance, that my hon. friend from Macleod, who I am sorry has just gone out, has more practical experience in banking than any economist who is not himself a banker. He has probably more experience than Sir Arthur Salter, and so said Sir Herbert Holt when he called the hon. gentleman one of his colleagues. "You are a banker yourself," Sir Herbert said to the hon. member. He admired the hon. gentleman's great experience in banking. But I am wondering how the central bank through inflation could increase the price of butter from twenty cents to sixty cents, how it could increase the price of cheese to twenty-five cents. How will the central bank through inflation restore the prices of commodities to what they were in 1930? And even if it did, it would not be the same, because the money would have less value; the currency would be less valuable. That is the point of view of a humble layman, a man in the street, looking at the theories put forward by hon. members in the extreme corner. They have been preaching these theories for a long time now and they may be sincere, but they are not practical; and what they tell us is a mere mirage. It is nothing but castles in the air, and it is a shame to tell the farmers that through inflation they will be richer than they are now. We must have a normal exchange of goods and we must come to that as soon as possible. In the meantime I hope that when hon. members in the far corner preach inflation they will be more convincing. I do not doubt their sincerity, but I say that they are preaching utopia, and it will make no one richer than he is now. I hope they will understand that it is much better to read the blue-
books and get acquainted with facts than to spend their nights reading the publications of economists of the old world and the United States, those dreams in books which always put one to sleep.
