speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman has not before him the statute as it was passed. The statute is chapter 24 of the statutes of 1930 assented to on May 30. It
exempted first of all dividends paid by one incorporated company to another. Then it dealt with cooperative companies and associations; it amended subsection 1 of section 5 by adding a description of dependent relatives ; it exempted ten per cent of the net taxable income in regard to donations and also exempted $5,000 of an annuity. Then, on page 233, section 19 was repealed and the following substituted:
19. (1) On the winding-up, discontinuance or reorganization of the business of any incorporated company, the distribution in any form of the property of the company shall be deemed to be the payment of a dividend to the extent that the company has on hand undistributed income earned in the taxation period 1930 and subsequent periods.
What happened? Just as soon as this was passed they proceeded to distribute all the income earned prior to that time. That was the joker in the whole statute; it applied only to 1930 and subsequent periods, and they proceeded immediately to distribute the income earned prior to 1930. Many members of the house thought that was not what the statute meant at all, but that was what it did mean in practice. That was the situation dealt with by the amendment passed last year, which is being further dealt with here. If the hon. gentleman will look at the language he will see how that construction could be put upon it. As a matter of fact the hon. member for York-Sunbury was arguing that there should be no payment of income tax on the distribution of undistributed profits. That should apply to the payment of a dividend to the extent that the company has on hand undistributed income earned in the taxation period 1930 and subsequent periods. The ones antecedent to 1930 got off free, and it is certain they took advantage of that provision.

All hon. members in the house at the time agreed that this legislation was imposing am extra burden on the taxpayer. It may have been that in practice someone ingeniously worked out the other situation. But everybody had his eyes open when the act was passed. It certainly did impose taxes which were not imposed before, and imposed them back to January 1, 1930, instead of, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury mentioned, July 1, 1930. The hon. member said:
I do not see that it can make very much difference to the department in the matter of taxation. You are establishing a new principle that for thirty years has not been resorted to. You are foregoing all the unearned and undistributed incomes of companies of this character

Foreign Insurance-Mr. Ralston
down to the first day of January. Why not go a little further and make it the first of Juiy or the thirtieth of June, 1930? I do not see any reason in the objection urged by the minister that you cannot have a broken period. The amount of tax can be ascertained.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is unnecessary to say that the hon. gentleman is not the interpreter of the statute; he did not interpret the statute. Here is the form in which it passed.
The only objection was that it went back too far.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But it was for another reason altogether.
The objection was that it went back too far, and taxed funds which up to that time had not been taxable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But as I say now, in practice what happened was it enabled those who had accumulated vast surpluses which they had not distributed, to escape taxation. It began to operate for the 1930 period and thereafter, but not antecedently to it. Large accumulations had taken place prior to that time. The statute which passed freed from taxation all moneys accumulated as surplus, and not distributed to shareholders prior to January 1, 1930, and thereafter.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the third reading of Bill No. 50, to amend the Foreign Insurance Companies Act.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct the
attention of the house to one clause of this bill which, it seems to me, should not pass. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has had his attention directed to it-I refer to that clause making one provision of the legislation retroactive. I shall state frankly that my attention was drawn to it by the solicitor of a party to an action now pending in the supreme court. I refer to section 6 of the bill which reenacts section 9 of the original legislation but with a very important amendment. Section 9 as reenacted provides for certain proceedings in the case of companies proposing to register where their names conflict or are liable to be objectionable on account of conflict with the names of companies already registered.
Section 9 of the old legislation provided that if the name of any company applying to be registered was in the opinion of the 	;	| |
superintendent objectionable on the ground that the name of the company was that of a company registered under this act, or a name liable to be confounded with the name of any such company, then the superintendent might refuse to register. The amendment provides that the superintendent may refuse to register mot only if the name of the company is in conflict with the name of another company registered under this act, but also if the name is one which conflicts with that of a company registered under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932. The objectionable feature is that by subsection 6 of section 9 it is provided:
(6) This section shall be deemed to have come into force, and shall be construed and applied as if it had come into force, on the twenty-sixth day of May, 1932; and any appeal to the Exchequer Court of Canada which any company has since the said date taken from the refusal of the minister to grant the application of the company for registry under this act on the ground of an objection to the name of the company, whether finally disposed of or not, shall be reconsidered and determined on the merits under and in accordance with the provisions of this section."
There is only one case in point, but it raises a question of principle concerning which I have spoken before in this house, and in connection with which I have very definite ideas. My general position is that retroactive legislation is objectionable, and I submit that retroactive legislation which interferes with legal proceedings now pending is doubly objectionable. The situation in this particular case is that the Continental Assurance Company incorporated in Illinois applied two years ago to be registered in this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is the Continental
Life Insurance Company.

No, I believe it is the
Continental Assurance Company. It applied to be registered, and the superintendent of insurance refused registration. After discussions lasting about two years the solicitor took the matter to the Exchequer Court of Canada, to which court there is an appeal from the superintendent, with the result that His Lordship the President of the Exchequer Court of Canada allowed the registration, and that is the situation at the present time. The appeal to the exchequer court was allowed on February 22, 1934.
The crown was a party to that litigation. The Continental Life Insurance Company, a company in Canada, were the respondents in the case, and the crown intervened. Judgment was given allowing registration of the Continental Assurance Company in Canada. Costs were reserved. There was no appeal

Foreign Insurance-Mr. Ralston
by the Canadian company, but the crown appealed. The appeal by the crown from that judgment is now pending before the Supreme Court of Canada. As I understand the circumstances of the case, there is no suggestion that the Continental Assurance Company is not eminently worthy of registration in Canada. It has been said that the judge of the exchequer court suggested that perhaps retroactive legislation might be passed. I understand that suggestion is denied. Only a few days ago in a letter from the solicitor of the Continental Assurance Company I was referred to the fact that the judgment of the learned exchequer court judge as published in the reports and as it appears officially contains no reference whatever to retroactive legislation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is hardly correct.

My argument is that even if the court had suggested retroactive legislation it would have been quite outside its jurisdiction and quite outside its functions, because after all the question as to the advisability or otherwise of legislation is for the government and this House of Commons. The second point is that there are hundreds of cases in which decisions of courts have been given on statutes. I submit that if, after a decision has been given on a statute in a certain form, we attempt to pass legislation amending the statute and providing that the amendment shall be retroactive, we are creating a very dangerous precedent indeed, and I do not think that there is anyone who will more quickly agree with that on general principles than the Prime Minister himself.
In the second place, the suggestion was that counsel had offered to waive the statute and to try the matter as if the statute had been amended. As counsel pointed out, he may have offered long before the litigation started at all to have the matter dealt with on the merits, but the department refused absolutely to take that position. It refused to have the statute amended but preferred to go to the exchequer court and have the matter decided on the statute as it stood. Now decision has been given against the crown and it is proposed that this house shall amend the statute and take away from the Continental Assurance Company the fruits of its litigation. I say, first, on the ground that the matter is sub judice, that we should not pass subsection 6 but that the appeal should be allowed to take its course in the Supreme Court of Canada to which it has been taken-by whom? by the crown itself-and, secondly, I say that retroactive legislation is highly objectionable.
The government has decided to appeal to the courts and the litigants have accepted the courts as the tribunal before whom that appeal is to be heard. The crown even intervened in this action to get into the case, and now, having intervened and got into the case, it has appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada; but instead of going on with the appeal it comes to this house now and asks the house to amend the legislation in order that the litigant may be robbed of the fruits of his success. This section changes the law and it makes this change govern a case which has already been disposed of by the established institutions of the country, and it sends the litigant back to the exchequer court under a law entirely different from the law as it stood when he began his litigation. It is bad enough for a private litigant to ask parliament to amend a law while litigation is in progress, but it is a good deal worse when the crown does so. If there is any party that should abide by the decisions of the courts of the country it is the crown and those representing the crown by whom the king's judges are appointed in the first instance. I think this will appeal to hon. members of this house who believe in fair play. The game has been played, and the crown has lost; and what is now proposed is this. The crown says, "True, we have lost the game, but we propose now to revise the rules and have the game played over again."
I need hardly say that I have not the slightest interest in this matter except that 1 have had a good deal of correspondence from Mr. Gray w'ho was representing the Continental Assurance Company, and I told him I would bring the matter to the attention of the house. I am doing so in view of that promise, but I am doing it also because I believe that it is a sound principle that we should not interfere with litigation, and particularly should we not put in an act a provision which gives the crowm a right which it had not, a right which will defeat the objects of the litigation and rob the litigant of the fruits of his success, sending him back to the exchequer court.
What about the merits?-because after all the house is interested in that question. This Continental Assurance Company which is applying for registration in Canada is incorporated under the law of Illinois. It is licensed in thirty-five states and has been doing business since 1911. As a matter of fact it is much larger in assets and business than the Continental Life Insurance Company, which is the Canadian concern. It is, I understand, a reputable and substantial
Foreign Insurance-Mr. Geary

company. Mr. Gray offered, I believe, to add the words "of Illinois" to the name of the company to make sure that there would be no possible conflict, or to add the words "Head office in Chicago, Illinois," or something of that sort to distinguish it clearly from the Continental Life Insurance Company; and the assurance was given further to employ no agent associated with the other company. These offers were not accepted; they were delayed two years in registration, and what do we find now in connection with the registration of insurance companies in this country? There are a number of companies with very similar names. For instance, you have the Mutual Life Insurance Company of Canada and the Mutual Life Insurance Company of New York, as well as the Mutual Life and Citizens Insurance Company, Limited, all registered; the Union Assurance Society Limited and the Union Insurance Society of Canton, both registered; The Phoenix Assurance Company Limited and the Phoenix Insurance Company, the Prudential Assurance Company Limited and the Prudential Insurance Company of America; the Imperial Assurance Company and the Imperial Insurance Office, all registered under acts of Canada. Yet refusal is given when application is made to register the Continental Assurance Company because there is another company called the Continental Life Insurance Company, notwithstanding that the Continental Assurance Company offers to have itself known as the Continental Assurance Company of Illinois, so that there may be no question about it.
I do not know what the real reason is why the suggestion was not accepted that the act should be amended, but evidently it was not accepted and we are here attempting to reverse the decision made by the exchequer court by a judge appointed by the crown, and we are proposing to pass this legislation at the instance of the crown. It offends against the rules of fair play, and I say that on the merits there does not seem to be reason for it. We should pass this act, amend it for the future, but allow the litigation to take its course and the crown should carry its appeal to the supreme court and abide by the result.
I move therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe):
That Bill B of the Senate, being Bill No. 50 of this house, be not now read a third time, blit that same be referred back to the committee of the whole house with direction to amend said bill by striking out subsection 6 of section 6 of said bill.

Some days ago I laid on the table of the house a petition addressed by the Continental Assurance Company to this house, setting out the facts in more detail than I have given them, and dated May 31, 1934. To that petition I would refer hon. members.
Mr. G. It. GEARY (South Toronto): I have some slight knowledge of this matter though perhaps not full or accurate enough to enable me to add very much to the discussion. The decision of the exchequer court has been on a technicality and in no wise on the merits. All parties, including the applicants, were willing to have the application treated as an application on the merits of the proposal. That has not been dealt with in the judgment of the exchequer court. As a matter of fact what happened was this. By reason of a fault in the statute, conceded by all parties, the judge of the exchequer court was unable to hear the application on and did not go into the merits, and the Continental Assurance Company is not prejudiced in the slightest. It has been willing, and is willing now I should imagine, that the matter should be discussed on the merits. If the statute is amended the road will be clear for that discussion. I am not dealing with that phase because I know nothing about it; but this is not a case of retroactive legislation in the sense in which that term is usually used. Nothing has been done under the act; the company has never done business in Canada; and while its road is clear to some extent under the judgment of the exchequer court, it will have got no further on its way by reason of that judgment, nor will it be prejudiced by reason of what has occurred up to the moment if the bill is passed and the parties present the case on the merits.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was placed in charge
of this bill when it came from the Senate. It was read the second time in this house, the house went into committee thereon and the bill was passed without any objection. Later the hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mouth (Mr. Ralston) intimated that Mr. Gray desired to be heard. He filed a petition which has been laid on the table of the house. The statements which the hon. gentleman has just made were the statements presented to the government in Mr. Gray's brief. However, even as Mr. Gray failed to make the matter clear upon the facts in his petition to the government, so has he not quite accurately stated the matter to the hon. gentleman. In order that there may be no misunderstanding and that the position

Foreign Insurance-Mr. Bennett
of the government be made perfectly clear,
I propose to quote from the judgment of the president of the exchequer court. What has been said by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. 'Geary) indicates clearly that this is not retroactive legislation in the ordinary sense; it is merely legislation to put the parties in the position in which it was always intended they should be and in which Mr. Gray himself asked on more than one occasion that they be put in until after he got judgment from the exchequer court.
That was before the litigation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I quote:
Maclean, J.:
Judgment rendered February 22, 1934.
The Continental Assurance Company, which for the sake of brevity and clarity will hereafter be referred to as the applicant, made application in October, 1932, to the superintendent of insurance, for its registration under the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, 1932. The applicant is a United States corporation, incorporated under the laws of the state of Illinois, and has carried on a life insurance business in a substantial wray in that country since 1911, and presently is licensed to carry on such business in thirty-five different states. The applicant, it is said, is associated, through share ownership with the Continental Casualty Company which is licensed to carry on business in Canada, and in fact does so, but that does not appear to have any relevancy to the issue to be determined here.
The applicant complied with all the requirements of the statute, and of the Department of Insurance, in its application for registration. After a hearing by the Superintendent of Insurance at which the applicant, and the Continental Life Insurance Company as an objecting party, appeared, the superintendent made a report to the Minister of Finance recommending that the registration of the applicant be refused on the ground that its name was liable to be confounded with the name of the Continental Life Insurance Company. a Canadian corporation licensed to carry on the business cf life insurance in Canada under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932, and thus "on public grounds objectionable"; thereupon the minister accordingly refused to register the applicant.
From the report of the Superintendent of Insurance and the refusal of the minister, the applicant appealed, and the right of appeal being questioned by the Superintendent of Insurance, the applicant applied to Angers, J. for an order requiring the Superintendent of Insurance to deliver to the applicant a certificate in writing setting forth his ruling in the matter of the applicant's application for registration and the reasons therefor, with which order the Superintendent of Insurance in due course complied. In the facts of this case, I think, there was the right of appeal under the statute.	.
Coming now to the real question for decision in this matter. The issue seems to me to be one of the interpretations of a statutory provision, and that is section 9 of the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, 1932, and it reads thus:
" If the name of any company applying to be registered is that of any company registered under this act, or, in the opinion of the superintendent, any name liable to be confounded therewith, or otherwise on public grounds objectionable, the superintendent shall so report to the minister, and the minister may refuse to register the company."
"(2) Such report, if based upon the objection that the name of the company applying to be registered is that of any company registered under this act or any name liable to be confounded therewith, shall be deemed to be a ruling of the superintendent from which an appeal shall lie under and subject to the provisions of section thirty-four of this act."
The Superintendent of Insurance, and the applicant, agree that the language of section 9 (1) is defective and through inadvertance does not express fully what was intended, that is to say, it was never intended by the legislature to limit the application of this statutory provision to companies registered under the Foreign Insurance Companies Act but should have included companies registered under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. The applicant, it is said, through the appropriate avenue, requested that this defect be cured by amending legislation. All parties to the controversy therefore agreed that something was omitted from the section of the act.
I direct the attention of the house to this:
Mr. Gray, for the applicant, agreed that I might construe this section of the act as if the omission had been supplied, and that I might deal with the appeal upon the merits if I felt inclined to do so. He, however, urged that upon a fair construction of the section as it stands the ruling of the Superintendent of Insurance was in error.
There can be no doubt, I think, as to the construction to be put on section 9. It means that a registration may be refused if the name of the applicant company is so similar to the name of a company already registered under the same act, as to cause confusion. The first clause of the section enables the superintendent to report adversely to an application of a foreign company for registration under the Foreign Insurance Companies Act on account of the similarity of its name to another foreign company already registered under the same act.
To attempt to sustain the refusal to register the applicant under the words "or otherwise on public grounds objectionable" is untenable, in my opinion. These words have no reference to the situation produced by an applicant company seeking registration under a name so similar to a name already registered as to be calculated to cause confusion. The words "or otherwise on public grounds objectionable," as here used, mean something other than the question of confusion arising out of the similarity of names and in such a case there is no appeal from the report or decision of the superintendent of insurance, while in the other case there is an appeal and an applicant is entitled to a judicial decision as to whether its name is liable to be confounded with another name. The words " or otherwise on public grounds objectionable " exclude an objection grounded on a possible confusion of names.
Foreign Insurance-Mr. Bennett

These are the important paragraphs:
Mr. Gray for the applicant, as I have already stated, expressed his willingness that I dispose of the appeal upon the merits if I so cared to do, and that I might assume that the alleged missing words were supplied in section 9 of the act in question. I do not think this is a case where the court would be justified in reading into the section the words said to have been inadvertently omitted. I think I am bound to assume that the legislature meant precisely what it said notwithstanding counsel for the applicant, and the superintendent of insurance, believe it to be a causes omissus. This is not a case where the imperfect wording of a section of a statute creates some doubt as to its meaning but where the intent of the legislature may be resolved with confidence from other provisions found in the same statute.
It seems to me that the appeal should be allowed and it should be declared that the applicant is entitled to registration. The statute, as it stands, authorizes a refusal of registration of a foreign insurance company under the act in question here when its name is liable to be confounded with the name of another foreign company already on the registry,-
This is not a foreign company already on the registry; that is really the gist of it. The judgment continues:
-and any attempt to base the refusal upon the words "otherwise on public grounds objectionable," does not appear tenable to me.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth is quite correct in saying that the following paragraph does not appear in the supreme court and exchequer court reports. It does not appear because it has nothing to do with the reasons in the case; it has reference only to this particular case and, therefore, is not important. In the certified case before the court this paragraph was included, as it should be, at page 57. It reads:
I cannot see any useful purpose now to be served in a discussion of the appeal upon the merits of the case. If the legislature amends the statute, the matter may, if desired by the parties interested, be brought before the court upon the merits upon the present record and without further argument; and, if I may properly do so. that aspect of the appeal is for the present reserved as is also the question of the costs of this appeal.
That is as clear a statement of this case as it is possible to conceive. That paragraph is not in the published law reports of the country because it has reference to this particular company and not to jurisprudence. But in the formal order settled by the court which can be changed only by the appeal are these words:
In the Exchequer Court of Canada Thursday, the 22nd day of February, A.D. 1934.
Present:
The Honourable the President
Then it recites the case and the name.

The appeal of the above named applicant coming on for hearing at the city of Ottawa, on the twenty-first day of November, A.D. 1933, before this court, in the presence of counsel for the applicant, for the Attorney General of Canada and for The Continental Life Insurance Company, intervenant, whereupon and upon hearing what was alleged by counsel aforesaid this court was pleased to direct that this appeal should stand over for judgment and the same coming on this day for judgment.
1.	This court doth order that the appeal from the ruling of the superintendent of insurance be allowed.
2.	And this court doth make no order as to costs of this appeal, but reserves this question-
The word "to" is left out.
-be dealt with upon the further proceedings, if any, in this court.
If that is not a clear indication and almost invitation to pass tlhis legislation I cannot conceive of anything clearer. What is more, in the formal judgment of the court provision is made for it. So, when this statute is enacted, the merits of the case will then be considered in accordance with the recommendations made by the learned judge as well in his reason for judgment as in the order which is based on those reasons. I cannot under the circumstances think the hon. gentleman is correct in describing this as retroactive legislation. It is legislation which counsel for the parties contemplate might be passed.
Not after litigation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am only reading from the judgment of the judge who says that counsel said to him: Give us judgment as though you were on the merits. He said: I cannot do that, but if the legislature intervenes, I. will do it. The legislature is now going to intervene.
He has to give two judgments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The judge said: I will not give judgment on the merits because it is clear I cannot read into the statute, even by consent, something that is not there. In other words, jurisprudence cannot be determined by a private arrangement. That being so, the learned judge contemplated that the statute would be passed. When it is passed, what happens? Have we taken away any man's rights? What we have done is to say to him: Let us hear the case on the merits, it not having been heard on the merits because the statute contemplated confusion with respect to another foreign company and not a domestic company and the domestic company is urging the confusion with respect to its position. For instance, in the daily papers the other evening it was reported that another

Foreign Insurance-Mr. Lapointe
continental insurance company had gone into the hands of the receiver. I asked my hon. friend if he knew anything about it. I did not know about it so I made inquiries and it was a company of a somewhat similar name in another state in the United States. That has nothing to do with this particular question which is purely and simply whether all parties having agreed during the trial that there should be a decision in the merits, this statute affords an opportunity for that decision to be made upon the merits of the case.

I believe with the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) that this bill contains a provision which is certainly unprecedented and the like of which cannot be found in any statute of this country. Let me read subclause 6 of clause 6 of this bill:
This section shall be deemed to have come into force, and shall be construed and applied as if it had come into force, on the twenty-sixth day of May, 1932; and any appeal to the Exchequer Court of Canada which any company has since the said date taken from the refusal of the minister to grant the application of the company for registry under this act on the ground of an objection to the name of the company, whether finally disposed of or not, shall be reconsidered and determined on the merits under and in accordance with the provisions of this section.
This is retroactive in two features; it is retroactive with regard to paragraph (a) of subclause 1 of clause 6 in which it is stated:
If the name of any company applying to be registered is in the opinion of the superintendent objectionable on the grounds that the name of the company is either-
(a) that of any company registered under this act or of any corporation registered under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932.
The act of 1932 said:
If the name of any company applying to be registered is that of any company registered under this act, or, in the opinion of the superintendent, any name liable to be confounded therewith.
By paragraph (a), this is added:
Or of any corporation registered under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932.
This widens the scope of this provision, making it applicable to something which was not in the act of 1932. Then subclause 5 provides that there shall be an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada from any judgment of the exchequer court under this measure. This was not in the act of 1932 and it comes after there has been litigation. There has been a legal action which has been decided by the exchequer court and which
is actually pending before the Supreme Court of Canada. The Prime Minister quoted the notes of judgment of the justice of the exchequer court and he admitted that the last two sentences, which are the most important to support his side of the present debate, are not in the official reports. Not only are they not in the official reports, but those sentences have been struck out from the official record. After inquiry was made in the office of the exchequer court it was found that the learned judge of that court had removed from the official record those two sentences.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to read that?-because I should be glad to know of a judge doing so.
Is it not in the official report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, this is the certified
copy.

I am advised by the
representatives of the Continental Assurance Company that after inquiring at the office of the exchequer court they found out that those words had been removed there too.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That makes the situation worse.

It makes it worse for
the case of my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does the former Minister of Justice say that a judge of a court, after a case has been passed for review in the supreme court, has changed his judgment?
Those are merely notes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I gave the formal judgment, as certified.

Those are reasons for
judgment. I am merely asserting what my information is; I have not seen it myself, but the solicitor for the company informed me that what I have stated is so. Does it not, however, look extraordinary that such a clause should be in this bill and that there is no provision for costs or anything in it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But the judgment has
reserved costs.

They will have to go
there and apply for them. By this bill if it becomes law the parties are put out of court altogether; they have no case left. They have been awarded judgment under the statute of 1932, and in 1934 we are enacting
Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

a law which says that this clause of the bill shall be deemed to have been in force since 1932; it is retroactive. This is certainly a vicious principle, however you look at it, and I shall support the amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston).
Amendment negatived on division.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Gobeil in the chair.
Penitentiaries-Amount required to carry out agreement between His Majesty and the municipality of the village of St. Vincent de Paul for extension of the present water and sewer system connected with St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, $3,000.
The Minister of Justice stated that when the estimates came up again he would have a report in connection with the hours of labour worked in the penitentiaries. I wonder if he has the statement now.

speechtext:
Yes, I have a memorandum in regard to the hours of labour of guards.
Under the present arrangement in all penitentiaries there are three shifts of guards of two as formerly. The time of the various shifts is as follows: The first shift is on from 7 a.m. to 6.15 p.m. Another shift comes on in the afternoon at 4.30 p.m. and remains on until 1 a.m. The third shift comes on at 12 midnight and remains on duty until 8.30 a.m. These are now known under present penitentiary regulations as the night watch, the morning watch, and day duty. It will be observed that day duty, from 7 a.m. to 6.15 p.m. is the long shift.

Has that been put into effect
in all the penitentiaries, and if so how many extra men have been put on the payroll?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is now in effect in
British Columbia, in Saskatchewan, at the Kingston penitentiaries and at Dorchester; and arrangements are now being made for Stoney Mountain and St. Vincent de Paul.
Did it necessitate the addition of any further employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Throughout all penitentiaries it will require sixty-six additional guards.

Would the
minister give some particulars regarding this item of $3,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This item is for the purpose of enabling us to construct an extension of a water main in the village of St. Vincent de Paul in connection with the penitentiary there. Part of the village of St. Vincent de Paul is on the penitentiary reserve. Has the minister any information regarding Piers island, how many Doukhobors are there now and what it costs?

For the year 1932-33	$170,783 82

Referring again to the
hours of work in the penitentiaries, if I heard the minister aright he said they are now having three shifts instead of two, but I notice that the day shift is still eleven hours and fifteen minutes. Could the minister tell us why the day shift is so long in view of the fact that they have three shifts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are more guards
on the day shift than on the night shift. The reason for that is that the men are out at work and the guards have to be with them in the various departments, and then they have to be there at seven in the morning for the opening of the cells and the serving of breakfast, and are kept on until supper has been served in the evening and the cells finally locked for the night. The shift that comes on at 4.30 in the afternoon assists the day shift until 6.15 and continues on until 1 a.m. So far the arrangement has proved very satisfactory from every standpoint, and I believe the guards themselves approve of it.

I wonder if the minister could say if the full day staff works the eleven hour shift.

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All on the day shift are supposed to work all day, and all on the other shifts are supposed to be on duty during the hours I have mentioned. There is supposed to be work for all.
I was wondering whether, because of the overlapping of some of the staffs, it might be possible that they were not all working, that some of them might get off earlier.

I would ask the minister if he would care to give the house a statement concerning the death of Sam Behan. I should like to know if convict Behan, who died recently, was paddled a few days previous to his death. I should like to know whether he was suffering from a heart condition and was under the doctor's care, and whether he had been given stimulants for some ten days before his death.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The late convict Behan was a life prisoner who had a very long criminal record. Originally he was confined in -the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary; he was considered of that class of prisoners who are rather dangerous, and that prison was not considered strong enough to restrain him if he made an attempt to escape. Consequently he was transferred to Kingston in the summer or spring of 1932. In the beginning of May- if my memory serves me, on May 3 last^-he created a disturbance in his cell in Kingston penitentiary of rather a noisy character. He smashed all the furniture in his cell, including his wash basin, dishes and the like, and turned on the water, flooding the cell. Some days later he was tried at the warden's court and awarded punishment, to consist of twenty strokes with a leather strap. On May 14 the punishment was carried out in the presence of the doctor, the warden and other officials, but only four strokes of the strap were administered. He asked to be relieved of the other strokes, and the warden granted his request. He thanked the warden and said that was the only good break he had ever had since coming to the institution. The other sixteen strokes were suspended; in that case they would not be adminstered unless the conduct of the prisoner in the future warranted it.
On May 26, early in the morning, it was reported in the office by one of the guards that Behan was complaining of being sick; that would be some time between six and seven o'clock in the morning. To keep myself accurate perhaps I might read some of the
statement made at an inquest which was held into the death of convict Behan. The first statement I will read is that of keeper Robinson, who was questioned by the crown attorney. He said:
Q. I understand you were on duty this morning when your attention was attracted to this prisoner?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. What hour would that be?
A. I would judge it would be between 6.30 and-
Q. Between six and seven o'clock?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. How long had you been on duty there?
A. From 12.30 in the evening.
Q. How was your attention attracted to the prisoner?
A. By the grating of a cup by one of the other inmates confined in the cells.
Q. Where were you at that time?
A. I was directly above, in the keepers' hall.
Q. Were you alone?
A. No, sir.
Q. What connection, if any, is there between the keepers' hall and the cells in which this man was confined?
A. If I can explain it in this way. Here is the keepers' hall, and the cells are directly beneath the keepers' hall.
Q. How are they reached?
A. There is a door at this end. You go down for four or five stairs, and then turn to your left, and down to the cells.
Q. What kind of door guards the exit from the keepers' hall when you step out of it?
A. The keepers' hall door is a steel barrier, sir.
Q. There is a steel barrier separating the keepers' hall from the outer world, through which you had to pass in going down to these cells?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. When you went out of the keepers' hall you passed through this steel barrier?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Then you descended four or five steps?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Then you turned to your left, and walked along-[DOT]
A. You turn to your left, and go down three or four steps.
Q. Then what do you do?
A. Then there is a light wooden door.
Q. What is the name of those cells?
A. They are generally spoken of as P.C., keepers' hall. Punishment cells.
Q. Then we are to understand that there is a light wooden door leading to the punishment cells below the keepers' hall?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Was that door closed when you reached there?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. And was there any other door except that wooden door on the punishment cells?
A. Inside, as you go through the wooden door, there is a barrier which screens this block off.
Q. What do you mean by a barrier?
A. A steel gate, sir.
Q. So that we have a wooden door, and beyond the wooden door there is a steel gate?
A, Yes, sir.

Q. And your attention was attracted, as you told us, by some noise that you heard. Was that first thing?
A. Yes, sir.	_
Q. Had you heard any previous noise?
A. No, sir.
Q. What did you do upon hearing that noise?
A. I immediately inspected, sir.
Q. What did you do?	_
A. I left the keepers' hall. Perhaps I might explain, sir. On taking charge at 12.30, it is customary for the keeper and the officer in charge, the assistant officer, to make alternate visits to the P.C. for safety, and as regards the welfare of the inmates, the last night, if I am not mistaken, we made nine visits from 12.30 to seven o'clock.
Q. What visits did you make yourself?
A. I was down and visited the P.C. at 12.40, 1.35, 2.15 and 6.30.
Q. The 6.30 visit, I surmise, being the one you made on hearing this noise?
A. No, sir. On my visit at 6.30 I was talking to convict Behan. He said, "Good morning, Keeper Robinson." I said, "Good morning, Behan." I said, "It's a little warmer this morning" and he said 'Yes, it is," and that's all that was said.
Q. And where were you when you were talking to him?	_
A. Directly in front of his cell.
Q. When you went in there, did you open this wooden door?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Did you open the steel gate?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. And you went along the corridor?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. And when you say you were standing in front of the cell that Behan was in, where was that?
A. As we go through the steel gate, we go right down to the end of the corridor where the cells are, and there is an electric clock. There are five cells in that corridor, and the electric clock is down at the end. Behan was in the third cell as I went in through the door.
Q. Was he in the left hand tier of cells?
A. On the west side. That would be my right hand.
Q. He was in the third cell from the door that you entered?
A. The steel gate.
Q. And there were five on each side?
A. There were five on this particular side.
Q. So that he was in the middle cell?
A. Yes, sir.	_
Q. And you say that when you went in and were talking to him, where were you?
A. Directly in front of his cell.
Q. Was he at that time lying down?
A. Yes sir, he was in bed.
Q. Was there any further conversation that occurred?
A. No, sir.
Q. And you fix that time as being 6.30?
A. I would say between 6.30 and 6.35.
Q. Did you have to punch any time clock?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Did you consult the clock since to find the time that you were there, to check up your time?
A. The idea is this. The time that is registered there, or any time clock throughout the prison, goes on a sheet.
[Mr. Guthrie.3
Q. Do you mean to say that when you punched the clock there, it would not be recorded there but would be recorded some place else?	_	_
A. It is recorded on the clock, and likewise recorded on a sheet.
Q. Then did you examine the record on that clock to find out whether it was 6.30, or do you fix the time from your own recollection?
A. No, sir. I make it my business to go down there between 6.30 and 6.35 every morning, before I leave.
Q. But I am asking you, did you check the time against the clock, or did you not?
A. No, sir, I am positive.	_
Q. I don't understand you. Are you positive that you did not check the time, or are you positive that it was 6.30, or what are you positive of?
A. I am positive that it was between 6.30 and 6.35 that I was in the hall downstairs.
Q. That is not based upon an inspection of the record, but it is based upon your recollection of the hour?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Will you continue, please. You were last telling us of this conversation. Then where did you go?
A. After the conversation I went back to the keepers' hall.
Q. And I suppose in doing so you locked the steel gate and closed the outer door?
A. Yes, sir.	.
Q. And would you then be alone in the keepers' hall?
A. No, sir.
Q. Who else was there?
A. Keeper Donoghue, and, if I am not mistaken, keeper Nolan was there.
Q. You think they would be there when you returned from this visit to the cells?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. So that there were three of you there?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Then how long after you heard this grating on the cup on the bars did you go back?
A. I went immediately, sir.
Q. About what time had elapsed since you had made your last visit?
A. I think it was about ten minutes from the time I had made my final visit until this grating was heard.
Q. And how long did it take you to go down to the cells?
A. A matter of a minute, sir.
Q. So you had been there ten minutes before?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. What did you find when you entered the
cells this time?
A. As I entered the wooden door, one of the convicts said that Behan was sick.
Q. We are to understand that Behan was not the sole occupant of the cells?
A. No, there were three others on the east side.	.
Q. Was Behan the only one on the west side?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. And then you started to tell us that when you went in the door one of these-do you know which one it was?
A. No, sir, I couldn't say for sure.
Q. What did he say?
A. That Behan was sick. They could hear him moaning.
Q. He said that Behan was sick, and he also said they could hear him moaning?
A. Yes, sir.

Q. Did you make any reply to that?
A. No, sir. I immediately went to Behan's cell.
Q. What did you find on arriving there?
A. Just as I have already stated, Behan was in bed, moaning, and he asked to see the doctor.
Q. What did you do?
A. I immediately returned to the keepers' hall, and in this time the deputy warden had arrived. I would judge it would be about 6.50. I reported the same to the deputy warden.
Q. What about the other men that were in the keepers' hall before the deputy warden?
A. They were still there.
Q. Didn't you see them before you saw the deputy warden-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Did you have any conversation with them?
A. I was speaking to them before I went down.
Q. What were you saying to them?
A. In connection with what, sir?
Q. In connection with what you saw downstairs?
A. I hadn't been down, sir. You misunderstand me.
Q. When you found Behan was in this condition in his cell, you told this jury that you came back to the keepers' hall?-A. I did.
Q. Who did you find there?
A. The deputy warden had arrived in the keepers' hall.
Q. The intelligent answer would be that the deputy warden was there, together with the men whom you left there, wouldn't it?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. You found the deputy warden in addition to the guards in the keepers' hall when you returned?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Then what happened?
A. I reported it to the deputy warden.
0. What followed that?
A. The deputy warden asked to have the hospital overseer notified, and to report to the keepers' hall immediately.
Q. Was that done?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Who came?
A. Overseer McConnell.
Q. Where was he summoned from, do vou know ?
A. From the prison hospital.
Q. That would be another wing of the same building?
( A. After you go through the main dome in "A" corridor, it is on the west side of the main dome.
Q. It is all enclosed under the one roof, isn't it?
A. Practically, sir.
Q. Did the hospital attendant McConnell arrive on the scene?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. What followed that?
A. I was waiting for him at the main barrier leading from the keepers' hall into the main dome. I escorted him downstairs to Behan's cell, and I opened Behan's cell to admit the hospital overseer. He examined Convict Behan, and stated that the case was too serious for him, and to have the doctor notified.
Q. Did you hear any conversation between Behan and McConnell?
A. No. sir.
Q. What followed that?
A. I immediately returned to the keepers' hall and had the doctor notified.
Q. Was that Dr. Platt?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. I suppose he came from his home, did he?
res, sir.
Q. How long after that did he arrive?
A. I think he was at the prison at about 7.10.
Q. Did you accompany the doctor down to the cell?
A. No, sir.
Q. That is the end of your connection with it?
A. Yes.
Perhaps from that point I should give the doctor's statement.
I find the following in the evidence of Doctor G. A. Platt:
Q. Have you got the hospital record of this man?
A. He has never been a hospital patient, so there is no hospital file.
Q. Has he been receiving any medical attention at your hands?
A. Yes, he has.
Q. I am speaking of the last month?
A. Yes.
Q. What was it?
A. He complained' of being unable to sleep. Said he was nervous, and wasn't sleeping well.
Q. When would this be?
A. This was particularly in the last seven or eight days-the last ten days. I have taken him over myself a tablet of veronal dissolved in w'ater.
Q. Would it be correct to say that you saw him yesterday?
A. Yes. I was with him sixteen minutes.
Q. What time would that be?
A. When I came out from speaking to him it was 7.20 by the clock in the keepers' hall.
Q. Morning or evening?
A. In the evening.
Q. So that you saw him last before you were called this morning was about 7.20 last evening?
A. Yes.
Q. Did you prescribe for him then?
A. Yes, the same thing.
Q. How did you happen to go there this morning?
A. I was called from the prison.
Q. About what time?
A. Seven o'clock.
Q. And you arrived there approximately-
A. I think it was thirteen minutes after seven, or twelve, when I arrived.
Q. Did you go at once to see him?
A. Yes.
Q. Will you describe to the jury in what condition you found him?
A. He was lying on the bed in his cell. I picked up his wrist and could feel no pulse. I then asked him what was the matter. He made no answer. I couldn't feel any pulse. I looked at his eyes, tried to listen to his heart. There was no heart action audible, and he had no reflexes in his eyes. He did breathe twice in the next minute or two. I suppose it was just the last action of the blood and the respiratory centres and then he was dead.

Q. The man was practically dead when you reached there?
A. Yes, he was.
Q. In your daily treatment and visits to him, had you any knowledge of any heart affliction?
A. None.	.
Q. Was there anything indicative of it?
A. No, no symptom to suggest heart trouble, nor was there any heart trouble that I could detect by stethoscope. I have used that many times.
Q. When?
A. I think I spent more time with him than with any convict in the institution. In the last week I had no occasion to examine his heart at all.
Q. When did you last examine his heart?
A. I think the last time would be a little over two weeks ago.
Q. As the result of complaints received from him ?
A. No. Part of my professional duty.
Q. Just in the ordinary course of duty?
A. Yes, it was in the course of duty.
Then there is the evidence of Doctor Hay, assistant professor of pathology at Queen's university, who performed the autopsy. Without reading all his evidence I shall read the following:
I examined the body of Samuel Behan. He was a man about forty-nine years of age, well developed and well nourished. There were no marks on his body of recent occurrence, but he had some old scars, on the cheek, on his chin, one on each knee, and some tattoo marks on each forearm. There were no recent marks of any kind whatever. I then examined the body internally. I found the right lung showed some evidences of slight tuberculosis, well healed now. His left lung was free of any previous disease. The heart was about normal in size. The right side was filled with blood. The left side was more or less contracted. I found that the artery which supplies the left side of the heart, one of the most important arteries, was rather badly diseased, a condition which we know as atheroma. In common language you speak of hardening of the arteries. The artery supplying the left side of the heart is extremely important, and if it be plugged by disease a blood clot may form, which cuts off the nourishment of the left side of the heart, that is the muscle itself, and this interferes with the working of the heart, and frequently brings about immediate death. I found this artery in very bad condition indeed.
Coroner: Doctor, is there any physical way of diagnosing it during life? Might that have happened to a private individual in ordinary life without him even having suspected it or consulting a doctor?
A. Coronary thrombosis is in many cases an extremely difficult condition to diagnose previous to death, previous to an inspection of the body. In some cases it is almost impossible. The heart sounds may be normal. If anything does show, it sometimes shows by a little difference in the rhythm, the regularity of the heart, but a doctor might examine a man's pulse for quite a long tune and not notice it. In some, cases it is detected by a delicate electrical instrument, but even that might fail. I have known cases where a man died very suddenly, and he had been sick before, and it

could not be detected. In some of the more chronic types they do complain of pain-that is angina pectoris. But sometimes they die very suddenly without complaining at all.
Q. Would it have been possible, by any chance, for any treatment to have saved him?
A. Nothing can be done whatever to change the condition of this artery. We are absolutely helpless.
Q. You mentioned a clot, doctor, I think?
A. Yes, perhaps I might explain. When the inside of the artery becomes diseased a clot of blood is very apt to form on the surface of this diseased area. It is liable to form more especially at night, when a man is resting, and as soon as he is disturbed in the morning he is liable to break this clot up, and it plugs a small branch of this artery, and that means the end. If the artery is very fine he has what we call a heart attack, and takes care of himself, but if it is a big one then, of course the attack is severe enough that it kills him immediately.
The other guards who were there give practically the same evidence as Robinson. After hearing the evidence the jury brought in this verdict:
We find that convict Samuel Behan came to his death from natural causes, namely, coronary thrombosis, a condition which it is not possible to previously detect, and that nothing further could have been done, in the opinion of the jury, to save his life.
That was the finding on the evidence taken at the coroners inquest which was held in connection with the death of this convict.
I want to be sure of the dates. The paddling of Behan took place on May 4?

speechtext: No, May 14.
And when did he die?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May 26.
Is it usual for wardens to be so lenient? After they have pronounced sentence of twenty strokes, is it usual for the paddling to cease after the fourth stroke?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. I have known a great many instances that have come before me where, after two, three, four or five strokes the remaining strokes have been held in suspense, and as a rule they are not given afterwards because good behaviour usually fol-lowsj In this instance it was at the end of the fourth stroke.

According to the new regulations, commented upon very favourably by the minister the last time we were debating this question, paddling is no longer allowed on command of the warden but only after consultation with the Department of Justice. Was convict Behan paddled before or after consultation with Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: After. All cases are now submitted to headquarters before paddling or strapping can take place. The evidence is also submitted.
After May 15 and until May 26, the day on which he died, was he confined to the isolation cell in which he slept on the floor or was he in his own cell?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He was in the punishment cell under the keeper's hall.
That was between those two dates. Had he been in the punishment cell prior to the fifteenth?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

I am sure the minister must have felt the death of Sam Behan under the circumstances. The report is elaborate but it does not convince me that Sam Behan was known to be a perfectly healthy man. We know all about the clergymen who went through the penitentiary and said that everything was all right; but the conduct of the penitentiary since that time has shown clearly that everything was not all right so that the jury's report does not mean as much as it might have meant before that occurrence. In the judgment of Judge Deroche in the case of Rex versus Kirkland, Behan was spoken of rather well in connection with the riot. On page 7 we find the following:
Two men, Garceau and Behan, addressed the crowd and told them to do no violence or injury to property.
That was brought out at least twice. It may be that Behan's death came unexpectedly and that nothing could have been done to save him, but as a member of this house I do not feel comfortable about it, when we know that he was paddled very shortly before his death, that he was in an isolation cell at the time of his death and that he did not have attendance, which might of course have happened to anyone. Coming as it does after the very real difficulty in both Kingston and St. Vincent de Paul, it seems to me to be one more strong argument in favour of a careful and impartial investigation into the conduct of our penitentiaries.
There were several other things I wanted to ask the minister. I understand that a very large number of men, thirty-six, I believe, were paddled just after the visit of the governor general to Kingston. There was some sort of demonstration in the penitentiary, a flooding of the whole ground floor, due I believe to an incident within the penitentiary; but possibly the official mind, which works in a peculiar way, may have associated
this with the official visit. From the information I have I should judge that the visit of His Excellency had nothing to do with it, but afterwards thirty-six men were paddled. Things may have gone very badly at the penitentiary, discipline may have broken down entirely, but I am not at all convinced that the paddling of thirty-six men, wholesale punishment in this way, will accomplish very much. Did consent for the paddling of these thirty-six men come from Ottawa or was it done on the warden's initiative?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
On the date in question
the governor general happened to be at the military college in Kingston, and word in some way was received amongst the prisoners that His Excellency was in Kingston and a communication was passed around, a copy of which was obtained, informing certain of the prisoners that this would be a good day to put on a demonstration. On the evening of that particular day, which I believe was the beginning of May or the end of April, a very noisy outbreak took place. It started with the rattling of trays or aluminum dishes and the flooding of as many cells as they could possibly flood in certain tiers of the building. It was a very noisy demonstration indeed. I do not want to give the names of the various prisoners, but twenty-two were awarded corporal punishment. The doctor pronounced two of them unfit and the rest were sentenced to various numbers of strokes.
